message:
To improve observability, this PR names six async I/O tasks that showed
up as UnnamedTask because they didn't override TaskType(). Each now
returns its class name: `ReadAheadIOTask`, `FileOpenTask`,
`AsyncWriteQueueTask`, `AsyncTaskQueueTask`, `FetchBlockTask`, and
`ReadRangeTask`.

This only changes the name the tasks report. Their behavior is
unchanged.

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Fixes https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/issues/28909

`HivePartitioning::ApplyFiltersToFileList` copied every filter for every
file, substituted the file's partition values as constants and evaluated
the result with `ExpressionExecutor::TryEvaluateScalar`. That creates a
new `ExpressionExecutor` per (file, filter), so functions with expensive
local state rebuild it for every file - e.g. `day()`/`month()`/`year()`
build a 29,584-entry `DateLookupCache` each time, making pruning ~10x
slower than with `dayofmonth()`.

This PR evaluates each filter with a single executor over all files:

* The partition/filename column references of each filter are rewritten
once into `BoundReferenceExpression`s into an input chunk (replacing
`ConvertKnownColRefToConstants`).
* The partition/filename values of all files are loaded as (unescaped)
strings into a VARCHAR `DataChunk`, one row per file, and the column
references are wrapped in a cast to the partition type, so no `Value` is
created per file and the cast runs as part of the filter. The filter is
run with `SelectExpression` per `STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE` batch.
`SelectExpression` is used rather than `ExecuteExpression` since some
internal table filter functions (e.g.
`__internal_tablefilter_selectivity_optional`) only have a select
callback.
* Whether a filter can be evaluated on partition values only (no
volatile functions, parameters, subqueries, other columns, ...) is still
decided by the existing `IsScalar()`/`IsFoldable()` check, done once per
filter.
* If evaluating a batch throws (e.g. a cast that fails for some
partition values), the batch is split in halves recursively, so only the
files for which the filter throws are kept (and the filter is preserved)
while the other files are still pruned. A single bad value costs
~2*log2(2048) extra evaluations for its batch only. A partition value
that cannot be cast to its `hive_types` type therefore no longer errors
during pruning - the scan still raises the same `Unable to cast ...
(from hive partition column ...)` error when it reads the file, unless
another filter prunes that file.
* The NULL marker / unescape handling is shared with
`HivePartitioning::GetValue`.
* The order of `file_filters` and of the preserved filters is unchanged.

#### Timings (10,000 hive partitions, none match, reldebug)

| filter | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `day(date) = 40` | 2.32 s | 0.22 s |
| `month(date) = 13` | 2.12 s | 0.23 s |
| `year(date) IN (1990, 1991)` | 1.24 s | 0.21 s |
| `dayofmonth(date) = 40` | 0.78 s | 0.22 s |

Added `test/sql/copy/partitioned/hive_partition_filter_evaluation.test`,
covering date part pruning, mixed partition/regular column filters,
volatile filters, filters that throw for some partitions, cast errors,
escaped values, NULL markers and filename filters, and
`hive_partition_filter_evaluation_large.test_slow`, which checks that
one throwing partition value among 2100 files still prunes the rest of
its batch (6/2100 files scanned).
subject: Evaluate hive partition filters with one executor per filter (#28957)
title: Evaluate hive partition filters with one executor per filter

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Moves six more settings to generic settings, and adds the small
framework piece needed for settings whose default is computed rather
than a constant.

**Computed defaults**
A generic setting either has a constant `default_value` or
`"default_function": true`. With the latter, the generator emits `static
Value GetDefaultValue(const DBConfig &config)`, which
`ConfigurationOption::default_function` points to. While the setting is
unset, `Settings::Get`, `current_setting` and `duckdb_settings()` return
the computed value. `RESET` (SQL and `DBConfig::ResetOption`) runs
`OnSet` with the default so it is applied, then clears the setting. No
placeholder is stored at startup. The default thread count is cached in
`DBConfig`, since it reads the cgroup CPU limit.

**Converted**
- `threads` / `async_threads` (default function, the system thread
count; `OnSet` validates and pushes to the `TaskScheduler`,
`DBConfig::options.maximum_threads` / `async_threads` removed)
- `max_memory` (`OnSet` parses, pushes to the buffer manager, keeps
`options.maximum_memory` as the exact parsed cache and stores the human
readable form as before)
- `http_proxy` (default function, the `HTTP_PROXY` environment variable;
`options.http_proxy` removed)
- `storage_compatibility_version` (default `latest`; `OnSet` validates
and keeps `options.storage_compatibility`, which holds more than the
string, in sync)
- `max_streaming_buffer_size` (default `10.0 MiB`,
`ClientConfig::max_streaming_buffer_size` removed; the value is parsed
where the buffer is created). It now keeps the string the user typed,
like `checkpoint_threshold`. `RESET` no longer clamps to the available
memory, which the old code only did on `RESET`.

**Still not converted, and why**
- `standard_vector_size`: compile-time constant with a read-only getter,
nothing to gain.
- `operator_memory_limit`: default is NULL (unlimited), which a generic
default cannot express yet.
- `max_temp_directory_size`, `temp_directory`: the reported value comes
from the live buffer manager, and `temp_directory` is coupled to
`use_temporary_directory` and the database path.
- `secret_directory`: state lives in `SecretManager`.
- The rest of the list in Robinho-MR/duckdb#316 is unchanged.

Tests: tests that assigned the removed fields now use `Settings::Set`;
`SET threads=0` now fails when set on the config instead of at open. New
cases in `test/sql/settings/generic_migrated_settings.test`;
`max_streaming_buffer_size.test` expects the raw string.

Default `unittest` suite on a RelWithDebInfo build: all pass except 29
tests that need loadable extensions that were not built, or a
symlink-free temp dir (`/dev/shm` path join); none touch these settings.
subject: Migrate computed-default settings to generic settings (#28955)

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
Add the remaining scan-affinity piece from [*Morsel-Driven
Parallelism*](https://db.in.tum.de/~leis/papers/morsels.pdf) to DuckDB.
Thanks to Leis et al.!.

Ready native table-scan jobs prefer workers near their cached blocks,
with work stealing to balance load. Affinity selection works
independently of asynchronous read-ahead, and workers reuse their scan
state across assignments.

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
A self-recursive macro with typed parameters crashes the process instead
of raising the expression depth error:

```sql
SET max_expression_depth = 50;
CREATE MACRO mt(x INTEGER) AS x;
CREATE OR REPLACE MACRO mt(x INTEGER) AS mt(mt(1));
SELECT mt(1);
-- segfault (stack overflow)
```

The untyped equivalent, `CREATE MACRO m(x) AS m(m(x))`, fails
immediately with `Max expression depth limit of 50 exceeded`.

When a candidate macro has typed parameters,
`MacroFunction::BindMacroFunction` binds the call arguments to pick an
overload. It does so in a fresh `ExpressionBinder` constructed on the
same `Binder`. `ExpressionBinder::InitializeStackCheck` starts that
binder at `INITIAL_DEPTH` (5) or at the depth of the enclosing subquery
scope, not at the depth of the call that is being bound.

For `mt(mt(1))` the argument `mt(1)` is bound in the probe binder, which
unfolds it to `mt(mt(1))` and probes `mt(1)` again in another fresh
binder. Every probe restarts at depth 5, so the checked depth alternates
between 9 and 13 and never reaches the limit. Binding recurses until the
C++ stack overflows. The argument stays constant after parameter
replacement, so nothing else grows either.

`BindMacroFunction` takes the calling `ExpressionBinder` and the probe
binder continues its stack depth through
`ExpressionBinder::ContinueStackDepth`, the same mechanism type
parameter binding already uses. Scalar macro unfolding passes `this`.
Table macros pass no caller: their arguments are bound from the table
ref binder, and recursion through them goes through new `Binder`s, which
are bounded by the binder depth and the table macro recursion check.

The depth error is a thrown `BinderException`, so it propagates out of
the probe instead of being folded into the `HasError()` path that falls
back to `UNKNOWN` for the argument type.

The probe really binds the nested arguments, so its depth now counts.
When the macro body keeps its argument, the unfolded body binds the
argument deeper than the probe does, and the limit is unchanged: with
`max_expression_depth = 50`, `inc(x INTEGER) AS x + 1` binds up to 7
nested calls with and without this change.

When the body discards its argument, only the probe binds it. With
`drop_arg(x INTEGER) AS 1` at `max_expression_depth = 50`, main binds at
least 40 nested calls and this change binds up to 10, since each nested
probe now adds 4 levels. The default limit of 1000 still binds 12.

`test/sql/catalog/function/test_recursive_typed_macro.test` covers the
reproducer, typed recursion over a column argument, recursion through a
scalar subquery, recursion through a lambda body, mutual recursion
between two typed macros, a typed macro recursing through an untyped
one, a typed table macro whose argument recurses through a typed scalar
macro, and the default depth limit. The untyped self-recursive macro is
the baseline. Finite typed nesting, overload selection between `INTEGER`
and `VARCHAR`, and nesting close to the limit still bind. The
discarded-argument nesting is pinned at both limits. The file sets
`max_execution_time`.

Not addressed: a recursive CTE with `USING KEY` binds its key aggregates
with `Binder::CreateBinder(context, nullptr)`
(`bind_recursive_cte_node.cpp`). The null parent resets both the binder
depth and the expression depth, so a macro that recurses through such an
aggregate is still unbounded:

```sql
SET max_expression_depth = 50;
CREATE MACRO mr(x INTEGER) AS x;
CREATE OR REPLACE MACRO mr(x INTEGER) AS (
    WITH RECURSIVE r(k, v) USING KEY (k, max(mr(mr(1))) AS v) AS (
        VALUES (1, 10)
        UNION ALL
        SELECT k + 1, v + 1 FROM r WHERE k < 2
    )
    SELECT v FROM r WHERE k = 1
);
SELECT mr(1);
```

The reset is independent of the overload probe and needs a separate fix.

Overload probing binds each typed argument fully before the unfolded
body binds it again, so binding time doubles per level of nested typed
macro calls (`inc(inc(...(1)))` with 18 levels takes about 10s). This is
independent of the depth handling and unchanged here.
subject: Continue the caller's expression depth when binding typed macro arguments (#28935)

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
hunk_contexts: static FilterPropagateResult PropagateValueComparison(const Value &lmin, const V
message:
## The query shape

A filter or a join condition that compares a column that holds only
NULLs with another column or expression:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM cast_member c JOIN person p ON p.legacy_id = c.person_id;   -- legacy_id was never filled in
SELECT ... FROM cast_member WHERE note_id <> person_id;                     -- note_id is NULL in every row
```

Columns like this are common in real schemas: an optional foreign key
that a migration added and nothing populates yet, a column kept for
compatibility, a wide generated table of which only some columns are
used. Queries written by people or generated by tools join and filter on
them regardless. Such a comparison is NULL for every row, so the filter
keeps nothing and the join matches nothing, but today the plan still
scans, builds and probes.

## What happens today

Statistics propagation prunes a comparison by the value ranges of its
two operands. A column that holds only NULLs has no range, so
`PropagateComparison` returns "no pruning possible". The fact that the
column has no valid value is used in two places only: `x IS [NOT] NULL`
is folded, and a comparison with a constant that was pushed into a scan
is pruned by the table filter. A comparison between two columns, or
between a column and an expression, is kept.

## The change

During statistics propagation, when the statistics of an operand say
that it can be NULL and cannot be anything else, the comparison is
replaced by a `NULL::BOOLEAN` constant:

| expression | folded when |
|---|---|
| `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` | either operand holds only NULLs |
| `x BETWEEN a AND b` | `x` holds only NULLs |
| `x [NOT] IN (...)` | `x` holds only NULLs |
| a BOOLEAN function with default NULL handling (`LIKE`, `contains`,
...) | an argument holds only NULLs |

What follows from the NULL constant is the existing machinery: a filter
becomes an empty result; for a join condition `HandleJoinNeverMatches`
is used, so INNER / SEMI joins become an empty result, LEFT / RIGHT
joins keep the preserved side and get an empty other side, ANTI joins
keep their left side, and FULL / MARK / SINGLE joins are left as they
are. A predicate that is not a comparison but sits among the conditions
of a join (`ON a.id = b.id AND contains(a.v, b.s)`) is treated the same
way: when it is NULL or FALSE for every pair, the join cannot match and
is handled as above.

The folded comparison no longer reads its operands. Columns that nothing
else reads are removed from the scans by the unused-column cleanup that
already runs after statistics propagation removed a filter or a join
condition.

One addition outside the propagator: the early filter-statistics pass
(`FilterStatisticsOptimizer`, which runs before the join order) so far
only runs for plans with a multi-table filter. It now also runs when a
filter or join condition reads a scanned column that holds only NULLs,
directly or through projections, aggregate groups, set operations and
materialized CTEs, so that the empty result is known before the join
order is chosen and the remaining joins are not ordered around a join
that cannot match. The check costs one statistics lookup per compared
scan column. Columns computed by other operators (a window, an unnest, a
recursive CTE) are not traced to their scans: a comparison with such a
column is still folded by the regular statistics propagation, but only
after the join order was chosen.

There is no new optimizer switch: this is part of
`statistics_propagation` and is switched off with it.

## Preconditions

- Not `IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM` (NULLs compare equal there). Where the
existing simplification turns `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` into `=` because
the other side has no NULLs, the `=` is folded.
- Not a bound of a `BETWEEN`: with a NULL bound the result is FALSE or
NULL, which is not a constant.
- Not `COALESCE`, `CASE`, `OR`, `IS NULL`: these are not NULL for a NULL
operand.
- No operand may throw, be volatile or sit behind an expression barrier
(`CAST(varchar_col AS DOUBLE)`, `random()`): removing the comparison
would remove the error or the side effect. `TRY_CAST`, casts that cannot
fail and arithmetic that the statistics prove cannot overflow are fine.
- The statistics must say "has NULLs, has no valid value". Statistics of
an empty input (neither) are left alone, so plans over empty tables do
not change.

The claim "no valid value" is the one that the `IS NULL` folding and the
table filter pruning already rely on. The cases in which it could be
stale each have a test:

| case | behaviour |
|---|---|
| one non-NULL value among 10,000 rows | not folded, the row is found |
| `UPDATE` to a value and back to NULL | not folded while the value is
there, the row is found; 0 rows after |
| committed append of a non-NULL value | not folded |
| transaction-local append (one row, and several row groups) and
transaction-local update | the local statistics are merged: not folded,
the local row is found |
| transaction-local append of NULLs only | 0 rows |
| another connection's uncommitted append | not visible to this
connection: 0 rows here, 1 row in the other connection |
| a snapshot opened before another connection commits a non-NULL value |
the result of the snapshot: 0 rows before and after the commit, 1 row in
the next transaction |
| a snapshot that still sees a row another connection deleted, plus a
`CHECKPOINT` | the row is not dropped while a snapshot sees it: 1 row |
| a snapshot that still sees a value another connection updated to NULL
(one row, and every row of the column) | the rows of the snapshot |
| every row updated to NULL, then `CHECKPOINT` | the statistics know
that the column holds only NULLs: folded; not folded again after one row
is updated to a value |
| a prepared statement, the table changed between two `EXECUTE` | 0
rows, then 1 row |
| `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`, then `UPDATE` | 0 rows, then all rows |

Outside the test file, 33 queries were compared with and without
statistics propagation on a database that was checkpointed and reopened,
on Parquet files (one file, lists of files in either order, an empty
file first), through `UNION ALL`, `VALUES`, materialized CTEs, windows,
aggregates, the NULL-extended side of outer joins, `unnest`, `CASE`,
`COALESCE`, structs and lists: all results are identical.

One difference a user can observe besides speed: an error that another
conjunct or operator of the pruned plan would have raised is not raised,
because that part of the plan no longer runs. This is the behaviour of
the empty results that statistics propagation already derives from value
ranges; the test file pins one case of each.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE person AS SELECT i AS id, 'person ' || i AS name, NULL::BIGINT AS legacy_id FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE movie AS SELECT i AS id, 'movie ' || i AS title, 1950 + i % 70 AS year FROM range(500000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE note AS SELECT i AS id, 'note ' || i AS text FROM range(1000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE cast_member AS
    SELECT i AS id, (i * 7919) % 2000000 AS person_id, (i * 104729) % 500000 AS movie_id,
           i % 12 AS role_id, NULL::BIGINT AS note_id
    FROM range(20000000) t(i);

SELECT m.year, count(*)
FROM cast_member c JOIN movie m ON m.id = c.movie_id JOIN person p ON p.legacy_id = c.person_id
GROUP BY m.year;
```

Before:

```
PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY  Groups: #0; Aggregates: count_star()
  HASH_JOIN  INNER; movie_id = id                          ~16,468,003 rows
    HASH_JOIN  INNER; person_id = legacy_id                ~17,701,127 rows
      SEQ_SCAN cast_member  [movie_id, person_id]          ~20,000,000 rows
      SEQ_SCAN person  [legacy_id]                         ~2,000,000 rows
    SEQ_SCAN movie  [id, year]                             ~500,000 rows
```

After:

```
HASH_GROUP_BY  Groups: #0; Aggregates: count_star()
  PROJECTION  year
    EMPTY_RESULT
```

A LEFT join keeps its left side and no longer reads the other table:

```
-- SELECT count(*), count(p.id) FROM cast_member c LEFT JOIN person p ON p.legacy_id = c.person_id;
HASH_JOIN  LEFT; person_id = legacy_id
  SEQ_SCAN cast_member  [person_id]
  EMPTY_RESULT
```

Measured on the example database with the change switched off and on in
the same binary. Instructions are user-mode instructions of a
single-threaded run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, median of 3) minus
the 237 M of a `SELECT 1` on the same database; wall clock is at 8
threads on a shared machine and only indicative.

| query | instructions before | after | wall before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| the three-table join above | 163 M | 15 M | 0.008 s | 0.001 s |
| `... cast_member c JOIN person p ON p.id = c.person_id JOIN movie m ON
m.id = c.movie_id JOIN note n ON n.id = c.note_id GROUP BY n.text` | 495
M | 15 M | 0.015 s | 0.001 s |
| `... cast_member c JOIN cast_member c2 ON c.movie_id = c2.movie_id
JOIN person p ON p.id = c.person_id JOIN person p2 ON p2.legacy_id =
c2.person_id WHERE p.name LIKE 'person 1%'` | 4,881 M | 17 M | 0.075 s |
0.001 s |
| `SELECT role_id, count(*) FROM cast_member WHERE note_id <> person_id
GROUP BY role_id` | 613 M | 12 M | 0.005 s | < 0.001 s |
| the LEFT join above | 432 M | 382 M | 0.004 s | 0.003 s |

The executor already stops a hash join early when its build side has no
valid key, which is why the first numbers are small in absolute terms.
What the plan-level pruning adds is everything the executor cannot skip:
the scan and filter of the column, the joins that feed the build side of
a join whose probe side is the NULL column (third row), and a join order
that is no longer chosen around a join that cannot match.

## Regression check

TPC-H and TPC-DS at SF1 and SF10, change switched off and on in the same
binary:

- plans: 0 of 121 queries change at either scale factor;
- results at SF1 with 1 and with 16 threads: identical (one TPC-DS query
that divides two floating-point aggregates varies in the last digit
between runs of the same configuration at 16 threads; it is identical at
1 thread);
- user-mode instructions at 1 thread, median of 3, per query: no query
above 1.05x; totals 1.001 (TPC-H SF1), 1.000 (TPC-DS SF1), 0.999 (TPC-H
SF10), 1.000 (TPC-DS SF10);
- planning cost of the additional check: cold `EXPLAIN` of the 99 TPC-DS
queries, 1.0004x instructions in total (largest single query 1.010x);
TPC-H 0.999x.

Repeated at SF1 for the current state of the branch against a build of
its base commit: 0 of 121 plans change, results are identical with 1 and
with 16 threads, cold `EXPLAIN` costs 1.0001x instructions in total on
TPC-DS (largest single query 1.009x) and 1.001x on TPC-H, and
`scripts/plan_cost_runner.py` reports no differences on TPC-H.

## Tests

`test/optimizer/statistics/statistics_all_null_operand.test` (429
assertions): the six comparisons between two columns in filters,
`BETWEEN`, `[NOT] IN`, `LIKE` / `NOT LIKE` / `contains`, the NULL
constant in a projection, INNER joins with and without casts, a five-way
join that is gone before the join order, one condition of several, SEMI,
and LEFT / RIGHT / FULL / ANTI / MARK / SINGLE joins with their results;
the same join types with a residual predicate next to an equality,
residual predicates that must stay, and the scans without the columns
that only a folded comparison read; a LEFT join whose plan shows that
the comparison was folded before the join order, with the column read
directly and through a projection, a view, an aggregate, a set operation
and materialized CTEs; a negative case for every precondition above (`IS
[NOT] DISTINCT FROM`, a `BETWEEN` bound, `COALESCE`, `OR`, `CASE`, casts
that can throw, which keep the comparison in the plan, `TRY_CAST`,
arithmetic, `random()`, an empty table); the statistics cases of the
table above with two connections; views, aggregates, outer joins and
nested types above the column; and the plans with
`statistics_propagation` disabled.

Existing tests that change:

- `test/sql/join/iejoin/iejoin_issue_6861.test` runs an IE join over a
table whose column was updated to NULL in every row and pins `IE_JOIN`
in the plan. In the default in-memory run the statistics still hold the
old values, so nothing changes there; under the test configs that run on
persistent storage (and in memory after a `CHECKPOINT`) the statistics
know that the column holds only NULLs and the comparison is folded to an
empty result. The test is about executing the join over all-NULL input,
so it now disables `statistics_propagation` for those queries, which
keeps the join in the plan under every config. Its results are
unchanged.

No other expected plan or result changes. The whole fast test suite and
`test/optimizer/*`, `test/sql/join/*`, `test/sql/subquery/*`,
`test/sql/cte/*`, `test/sql/filter/*`, `test/sql/transactions/*`,
`test/sql/update/*`, `test/sql/delete/*`, `test/sql/types/list/*`,
`test/sql/unnest/*`, `test/sql/tpch/*` and `test/sql/tpcds/*` including
the slow tests pass. The new test is added to
`test/configs/stats_dependent_tests.json`, the list of tests that are
skipped when the optimizer is disabled because they depend on
statistics; it passes under the other test configs. The whole test suite
was also run under each config of `make test_configs` before the last
change. After it, the whole fast suite passes in the default config, and
the new test plus `test/optimizer/*`, `test/sql/join/*`,
`test/sql/subquery/*`, `test/sql/cte/*` and `test/sql/filter/*` were run
as follows: under the default config, `verify_column_bindings`,
`force_external`, `force_storage`, `latest_storage`, `verify_fetch_row`
and `stats_dependent_tests` all pass; under `force_storage_restart` two
slow recursive-CTE tests that read runtime logs fail
(`test/sql/cte/recursive_cte_flummi.test_slow`,
`test/sql/cte/recursive_cte_asql_ws2526.test_slow`: the logs do not
survive the restart; not compared with a build of the base commit) and
everything else passes; under `disable_optimizer` only the fast tests
were run, and one of them
(`test/optimizer/recursive_cte_cost_alternatives.test`) hits its own

hunk_contexts: void DatabaseHandle::Read(QueryContext context, FileBuffer &block, uint64_t loca
message:
A block id that is stored in the metadata of a database file is used
without looking at it. Two cases, both hit by `ATTACH` of a corrupt
file:

* The pointer to the next block of a metadata chain holds a very large
block id. `SingleFileBlockManager::GetBlockLocation` multiplies the id
with the block size, which wraps around. `DatabaseHandle::Read` then
decides whether the read can be served from the prefetched header with
`location + block.AllocSize() <= prefetched_header->size()`. That sum
wraps as well, the check passes, and one block is copied from outside of
the prefetched header buffer. AddressSanitizer reports the read; a
release build reports a checksum mismatch over whatever memory was
copied (the numbers in the message differ from run to run).
* The list of metadata blocks that is stored with the free list holds a
block id in the range of in-memory blocks: `INTERNAL Error:
AddAndRegisterBlock called with a transient block id`, which invalidates
the instance.

With this PR:

* `GetBlockLocation` throws `Data Corruption Error: Corrupt database
file: block id <id> is out of range` when the location of the block or
its end does not fit.
* The check in `DatabaseHandle::Read` no longer adds to the location.
* `MetadataManager::Read` throws `Data Corruption Error: Corrupt
database file: invalid metadata block id <id>` for an id that is
negative or in the range of in-memory blocks.

A block id that is in range but past the end of the file is not touched
here: reading it already fails with a regular error.

### Test

`test/sql/storage/corrupt/block_id_out_of_range.test` attaches one file
per case (`data/storage/corrupt/block_id_location_overflow.db.gz`,
`metadata_block_id_transient.db.gz`, 4 KB and 3 KB) and checks that the
instance is still usable afterwards. Both files were found by fuzzing
the storage reader. The test also passes under AddressSanitizer, which
reported the out-of-bounds read for the first file before the fix.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
## The query shape

A correlated `EXISTS` (or correlated `IN`) whose subquery also carries a
predicate on the outer key only:

```sql
SELECT ... FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.customer_id > 17000);
```

This is what query generators and hand-written reports produce when a
restriction on the outer row is written next to the correlation instead
of in the outer `WHERE`: the two places are equivalent for `EXISTS`, and
a view or a template often only allows adding conditions inside the
subquery. Written in the outer `WHERE`, the predicate is pushed into the
scan of `orders`. Written inside the subquery it is not: the outer rows
are produced in full and the predicate is only applied to the
duplicate-eliminated domain.

## What happens today

The subquery is decorrelated into a materialized CTE of the outer rows
with two references: the outer rows on the left side of a MARK join, and
the domain of distinct keys below the subquery. The predicate
`o.customer_id > 17000` ends up as a filter on the domain reference
only. The CTE filter pusher restricts a CTE only when every reference is
filtered, so the scan of `orders` stays unfiltered:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN orders  [customer_id, amount]                                ~3,000,000 rows
  FILTER  SUBQUERY
    HASH_JOIN  MARK; customer_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM customer_id
      CTE_SCAN                                                          ~3,000,000 rows
      ... HASH_JOIN INNER customer_id = customer_id
            (GROUP BY over FILTER (#[0.0] > 17000) over CTE_SCAN)
            SEQ_SCAN customers  Filters: customer_id > 17000
```

## The change

The change lives in the CTE filter pusher. Before it pushes the filters
of the references into a CTE, it treats a join that keeps only the
matching rows of a CTE reference as one more consumer filter of that
reference:

```
SEMI[l = r](CTE_REF c, R)                 ->  SEMI[l = r](FILTER[p(l)](CTE_REF c), R)
FILTER[mark](MARK[l = r](CTE_REF c, R))   ->  FILTER[mark](MARK[l = r](FILTER[p(l)](CTE_REF c), R))
                                              when p(r) is TRUE for every row of R
```

A left row survives a SEMI join, or a MARK join under a filter on the
bare mark, only together with a right row whose key equals its own. A
comparison with constants that is TRUE for the key of every right row is
therefore TRUE for the key of every surviving left row, and filtering
the left side by it first removes only rows that the join drops anyway.
With the filter on the outer rows' reference every reference of the CTE
is filtered, and the pusher moves the predicate into the CTE definition
as it does for any other consumer filter:

```
CTE __duckdb_delim
  SEQ_SCAN orders  [customer_id, amount]  Filters: customer_id > 17000  ~600,000 rows
  FILTER  SUBQUERY
    HASH_JOIN  MARK; customer_id IS NOT DISTINCT FROM customer_id
      FILTER (#[0.0] > 17000)
        CTE_SCAN
      ... (unchanged)
```

It is built from three parts:

- **Orchestration: `CTEFilterPusher::GenerateSemiJoinFilters`**, called
from `CTEFilterPusher::Optimize` right after it has collected the CTEs
and their references (implemented in
`src/optimizer/cte_semi_join_filter_transfer.cpp`). It uses the pusher's
own reference inventory to decide whether a reference qualifies (every
other reference of the CTE is filtered already) and records the new
filter there, so the push that follows sees an ordinary filtered
reference. It is part of the `cte_filter_pusher` optimizer and is
switched off with it.
- **Discovery: which filters hold for every right row.** A small search
follows the right join key down through filters, table filters of a
scan, column-reference projections, the groups of an aggregate, the
preserved side of joins and the equalities of INNER joins, and collects
the filters that compare that column with constants. It does not look at
the left side and does not rewrite anything. The positive-MARK case is a
separate check (`FILTER` with the bare mark as a conjunct over a MARK
comparison join) that only selects the join.
- **Transfer: `FilterCombiner::GenerateJoinFilters`**, unchanged, the
helper that `FilterPullup::PullupSemiJoin` and
`FilterPushdown::PushdownSemiAntiJoin` use. It derives the left-side
filters from the collected right-side filters and the join conditions;
the search also uses it for the equalities of an INNER join. Which
predicates can cross an equality is therefore decided in one place:
comparisons with constants, `BETWEEN` and `IN` lists (as
`FilterCombiner::GetComparedExpression` defines them). Predicates the
helper does not derive (`OR`, `IS [NOT] NULL`, `NOT IN`) are not
transferred.

`CTEFilterPusher::PushFilterIntoCTE` is unchanged. It restricts a CTE by
the disjunction of the filters of its references and hands that to the
expression rewriter, whose `DistributivityRule` reduces `(A AND B) OR A`
to `A`. The new filter usually repeats the filter of the other
reference, so it is added to the plan as one flat conjunction, which is
the form the rule reduces; the scan then gets `customer_id > 17000` and
not a disjunction. Nothing else simplifies the pushed filter, for any
CTE.

## Preconditions

- The left child of the join is a reference of a materialized CTE (bare
or under a filter), not a recurring or correlated reference, and every
other reference of that CTE is already filtered. The new filter is then
exactly what the CTE filter pusher was missing. Other left sides (for
example a plain table scan under an uncorrelated `IN`) are left alone.
- A SEMI comparison join, or a MARK comparison join directly under a
filter that has the bare mark as a conjunct. Not ANTI, outer, delim or
AsOf joins, and not a mark that is used in any other way (`NOT mark`,
under an `OR`, in the select list).
- The join condition is `=` or `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, with a bare
column on the right side.
- Only filters that compare the key with constants and cannot throw are
transferred: comparisons, `BETWEEN` and `IN` lists. A function of the
key, an `OR`, a NULL test and `NOT IN` are not.
- "Every right row passes it" is established conservatively: the
NULL-extended side of an outer join, grouping sets, set operations, CTE
references and optional scan filters end the search.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders AS
    SELECT i AS order_id, (i * 7919) % 20000 AS customer_id, DATE '2024-01-01' + (i % 365)::INTEGER AS order_date,
           ((i % 1000) / 10.0)::DECIMAL(10,1) AS amount, 'note ' || (i % 100000) AS note,
           i % 7 AS status, i % 13 AS channel, i % 101 AS store_id
    FROM range(30000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE customers AS SELECT i AS customer_id, 'customer ' || i AS name, i % 50 AS region FROM range(18000) t(i);

SELECT status, channel, count(*), sum(amount), max(note), min(order_date), max(store_id)
FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id AND <predicate on o.customer_id>)
GROUP BY status, channel;
```

Base of this branch against the branch, release builds. User-mode
instructions of a single-threaded run (`perf stat -e instructions:u`,
median of 3, including the 0.24 G of process start-up):

| predicate inside the subquery | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `o.customer_id > 17000` (15 % of the rows pass it, 5 % have a match) |
13.5 G | 5.8 G |
| `o.customer_id BETWEEN 100 AND 300 AND c.region < 25` | 13.1 G | 4.2 G
|
| `o.customer_id > 100000` (no row can match) | 9.4 G | 0.26 G |
| control: `o.customer_id > 17000` written in the outer `WHERE` | 4.5 G
| 4.5 G |

The control shows what is left on the table: with the predicate in the
outer `WHERE` the subquery is deliminated into a plain semi join. The
change does not rewrite the query into that form, it only stops the scan
from producing rows that cannot match.

## Regression check

None of the TPC-H and TPC-DS queries has this shape, so the two suites
are regression evidence only and the example above carries the case.
Base against branch at SF1:

- plans: 0 of 121 queries change;
- results with 1 and with 16 threads: identical (one query differs in
the last digit of a floating-point aggregate between two parallel runs
of the same binary);
- `scripts/plan_cost_runner.py` on `benchmark/tpch_plan_cost`: no
differences.

## Tests

`test/optimizer/cte_semi_join_filter_transfer.test` (434 assertions): 42
result cases over tables with NULL, duplicate and unmatched keys on both
sides (empty left / right side, null-safe correlation, `NOT EXISTS`,
`EXISTS` as a value, the mark under an `OR`, a predicate that can throw,
the NULL-extended side of a LEFT join, grouping sets, `UNION`, nested
`EXISTS`, correlated `IN`, VARCHAR and DATE keys, DOUBLE keys with
`0.0`, `-0.0` and NaN, references of a materialized CTE whose filters
differ only in the sign of a zero passed to `signbit`, query-written
materialized CTEs with one reference, a reference that is filtered
already, two filtered references and one unfiltered reference) and 24
plan pins: the predicate reaches the outer scan as a single filter for
`>` (also with a negative zero and under a null-safe correlation),
`BETWEEN`, `IN` lists, a second correlated column, a correlated `IN` and
a reference that is filtered already; it does not for `NOT EXISTS`, a
mark that is output or under an `OR`, a plain scan on the left side, a
function of the outer key, an `OR` or a NULL test on the key, the
NULL-extended side of an outer join, grouping sets, a CTE with an
unfiltered reference, and with the CTE filter pusher disabled. A last
block repeats result cases with the CTE filter pusher disabled.

Existing tests: no expected plan or result changes. `test/optimizer/*`,
`test/sql/cte/*`, `test/sql/subquery/*`, `test/sql/join/*` and
`test/sql/filter/*` pass, also with column binding verification, forced
external operators, forced storage and forced row fetches.

This PR touches `cte_filter_pusher.cpp` in one place (the call of the
helper) and adds one source file.

Relation to #28760 / #28639: those PRs change the filter dependency of
delim CTEs in the other direction and remove identity projections around
them; the plan pins of this test need to be re-run once they land.
Relation to #28732: once `FILTER[mark](MARK)` is a SEMI join by the time
the CTE filter pusher runs, the MARK check here is dead and can be
removed; the SEMI case covers it.

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
A transaction (and the local storage / optimistic writers it owns)
should not depend on the connection that created it, so that it can
later be shared between connections without keeping the creating
`ClientContext` alive.

### What changes
- `MetaTransaction` no longer stores a `ClientContext &`. It is created
from the `DatabaseInstance`; `GetTransaction`, `Commit`, `Finalize` and
`ModifyDatabase` take the context of the connection doing the work.
- `UndoBuffer` only needs the `DatabaseInstance`.
- `LocalStorage`, `LocalTableStorage` and `OptimisticDataWriter` no
longer store a `Context &`. Methods that need one (`InitializeAppend`,
`Delete`, `Commit`, `GetOptimisticWriter`, `CreateCollection`,
`WriteNewRowGroup`, `WriteUnflushedRowGroups`, `FinalFlush`, `Merge`,
...) take it as a parameter. `LocalAppendState` carries it for the
duration of one statement.
- `PartialBlockManager` takes the context for its IO as a parameter
instead of storing a `QueryContext`, so a manager that outlives or is
merged across queries never points at a dead context.
- The unchecked `Transaction::context.lock()` dereferences are gone:
`CommitState` uses an empty `QueryContext` (as the cleanup path already
does), struct/variant column casts use the database cast set.
- `Transaction::context` itself is left in place for out-of-tree
extensions; removing it needs per-extension patches (follow-up).

### Testing
Full `unittest` run (reldebug-style build, with the loadable test
extensions built): all pass. The only failures in the first run were
tests needing the demo extensions (not yet built at that point, re-run
and pass) and two environment-specific ones (`/dev/shm` temp-dir path,
port already in use), which pass when re-run without those. Not run:
`.test_slow` storage tests, `test_configs`, `test_vector`.
subject: Do not store the creating connection's context in transactions and local storage (#28953)

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
## What this applies to

Filters on a column whose values are stored in runs: an append-ordered
timestamp or date, an auto-incremented id, a table loaded sorted or
partition by partition. "The last day of an event log", "orders of one
quarter" or "ids above a watermark" select a contiguous slice of such a
table, and the scan already skips every row group outside that slice
through its zonemaps (the per-row-group min/max).

The planner does not use that information. A range filter is estimated
from the table-level statistics with the default selectivity of 0.2 as
its floor, so a filter that keeps 0.1 % of an append-ordered table is
planned as if it kept 20 %. The scan then looks two orders of magnitude
larger than it is, and the join order and the build side are chosen for
the wrong sizes.

## What changes

The estimate of a DuckDB table scan with table filters is bounded by the
rows of the row groups whose zonemaps can satisfy all of its filters.
The row groups come from the existing `get_partition_stats` callback
(what the row group pruner and the `count(*)` statistics shortcut
already read at plan time), and the per-row-group check is
`ExpressionFilter::CheckExpressionStatistics`, the check the scan itself
uses to skip a row group. This is a count, not an estimate: rows of row
groups the scan will skip are not returned.

A row group that cannot be skipped counts whole. There is no
interpolation inside a row group that a range cuts, so the bound is
exact to the row group and no finer: a range that ends inside a row
group is estimated at that row group's full row count.

The bound only ever lowers an estimate: it is combined with the existing
estimate by `min`, in `RelationStatisticsHelper::ExtractGetStats`, so
join ordering and standalone cardinality estimation both see it. A
column that is not clustered is untouched: every row group spans the
whole range and nothing is skipped. Row groups are counted with the rows
the planning transaction can see, so rows it has deleted are not counted
and rows deleted by a transaction it cannot see still are.

### Relation to #28341

#28341 interpolates integer ranges over the table-level `[min, max]`
(`IntegerRangeEstimate`) and keeps the default selectivity as the floor
of that interpolation. This PR does not interpolate and does not touch
that code: the estimate goes below 20 % of the table only through row
groups that are skipped whole. For a table of a single row group, or a
column that is not stored in runs, nothing changes, and the tests of
#28341 pass unchanged.

Interpolating inside the row groups that a range cuts would tighten the
bound further. That belongs in the shared range-estimation code (the
interval calculation of `IntegerRangeEstimate` applied to row-group
statistics, with the clustering checks and the floor outside it) and is
left for a follow-up; it also needs the types that matter most here
(DATE, TIMESTAMP), which `IntegerRangeEstimate` does not cover today.

### Relation to #28664

#28664 estimates the selectivity of a scan's filters on a row sample and
inserts that estimate at the same place, directly before
`ApplyFilterEstimate`. The two are complementary: a sample estimates any
filter on any layout, the zonemaps give a count for the rows a scan
cannot return. Both are combined with the existing estimate by `min`, so
they compose in either order; whichever lands second rebases those few
lines.

### Preconditions

* a DuckDB table scan (`get_partition_stats` with row group statistics);
other sources keep their estimate;
* at least one non-optional table filter without parameters on a regular
column (not the row id, not a generated column); optional filters do not
restrict the result and are ignored;
* every filter and type the zonemap check understands takes part
(comparisons, `IN`, `IS NULL`, string prefixes, ...);
* the table has at most 16,384 row groups (2 billion rows at the default
row group size). A larger table keeps its estimate: checking only some
of its row groups would not give a bound, because the row groups that
are not checked can hold all of the matching rows;
* the estimate is above one row. The walk also stops as soon as the rows
counted so far reach the current estimate, since the bound can no longer
improve on it.

No table data is read. For a table that was just opened, the zonemaps of
the filtered columns are loaded at plan time instead of at the start of
the scan, which needs them anyway.

## Example

```sql
-- an event log appended in time order: one event per second for about 579 days
CREATE TABLE events AS
    SELECT TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01' + INTERVAL (range) SECOND AS ts, (range * 7919) % 2000000 AS user_id, range % 100 AS kind
    FROM range(50000000);
CREATE TABLE users AS SELECT range AS user_id, 'user ' || range AS name, range % 50 AS country FROM range(2000000);

SELECT u.country, count(*)
FROM events e JOIN users u ON e.user_id = u.user_id
WHERE e.ts >= TIMESTAMP '2025-08-01'
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY ALL LIMIT 3;
```

The filter keeps 60,800 of 50,000,000 events, all of them in the last
row group (110,720 rows).

| | estimated rows of the `events` scan | actual | hash join |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 10,000,000 | 60,800 | builds on `users` (2,000,000 rows),
probes with `events` |
| after | 110,720 | 60,800 | builds on the filtered `events`, probes
`users` |

Timings of the query (release build, in-memory, best of 5, shared
machine):

| threads | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.054 s | 0.008 s |
| 8 | 0.015 s | 0.004 s |

Planning cost. The work per plan is limited to the row groups of one
table of at most 16,384 row groups, and the limit is tested on the row
group count before any row group is loaded or collected
(`DataTable::GetRowGroupCountWithoutLoading`, a small accessor this PR
adds; with the existing `GetRowGroupCountWithLocalStorage`, the first
plan on a freshly opened table of 100,000 row groups loads all of them,
108 ms instead of 4 ms). `EXPLAIN` time at 1 thread with the zonemaps in
memory, before / after, on tables of 2,048-row row groups with a sorted
`id`:

| row groups | `id = <constant>` | `id < 100000` |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 0.45 / 0.68 ms (estimate 2 rows) | 0.45 / 0.95 ms |
| 16,000 | 0.47 / 0.45 ms (estimate 1 row, not read) | 0.5 / 7.0 ms |
| 100,000 | 0.50 / 0.50 ms (above the limit) | 0.55 / 0.60 ms (above the
limit) |

The 16,000-row-group range query is the worst case under the limit:
about 0.4 µs per row group, the same check the scan makes for each row
group when it runs. The first plan after opening a database also loads
the zonemaps of the filtered columns (about 65 ms for 16,000 row
groups), which the scan otherwise does at its start.

## Regression check

The base commit vs this branch, release builds, one process per query
and build.

* TPC-H SF1 / SF10 and TPC-DS SF1 / SF10 as generated (not stored in
date order): EXPLAIN output, including every estimate, is identical for
all queries; `scripts/plan_cost_runner.py` on TPC-H reports no
differences. JOB: 13 of 113 queries get a lower estimate for one scan (a
string filter on a column that happens to be clustered skips row
groups); no plan shape changes.
* Results at 1, 8 and 64 threads on TPC-H SF1 / SF10 and TPC-DS SF1 /
SF10, and at 1 and 8 threads on JOB, are the same on both builds (one
TPC-DS query that divides DOUBLE aggregates matches at 1 thread and
varies from run to run at 8 and 64 threads, with identical plans on both
builds).
* User-mode instructions at 1 thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`,
median of 3), geometric mean branch / base: TPC-H SF1 0.999, SF10 1.001;
TPC-DS SF1 1.000, SF10 1.000; JOB 0.998. Four first-pass readings above
1.05 (1.06 to 1.08, all on queries whose EXPLAIN output is identical on
both builds) were re-run with 11 repetitions and came out at 0.90 to
1.01.
* The same data stored in runs (TPC-H SF10 with `lineitem` in ship date
order and `orders` in order date order, as an append-by-time load would
produce): the estimates of the date-range scans go from a q-error of 5.2
to 16.0 down to 1.15 to 1.29. 8 of 22 queries get different estimates, 3
plans change, results are identical at 1, 8 and 64 threads.

## Tests

* `test/optimizer/statistics/scan_selectivity_zonemaps.test`: ranges on
a sorted key and a clustered date (the rows of the row groups that are
left), a range inside one row group (counts whole), the same range on a
permuted column (no row group is skipped, the estimate of the table
statistics stands), a conjunction across two columns that only the row
groups refute, two cases in which the bound is above the existing
estimate and does not raise it, the results of all of these queries; and
the rows a transaction can see: its own inserts, an uncommitted update
(the zonemap of its row group widens at once), its own deletes, a
rollback, and a transaction that started before another connection
committed a delete (it still sees the rows, and they are still counted).
* `test/optimizer/statistics/scan_selectivity_zonemaps_guards.test`: one
row group selected exactly for INTEGER, a nullable column, `IS NULL`,
VARCHAR, DECIMAL and TIMESTAMP; the estimate of the table statistics for
a scan without filters, a Parquet scan, a filter no zonemap refutes, a
range on an unclustered column and a row id filter; an empty table; a
filter the table statistics refute keeps its 0 rows; a join whose build
side follows the estimate, in both directions; a table that was just
attached.
*
`test/optimizer/statistics/scan_selectivity_zonemaps_row_group_limit.test_slow`:
a table of 16,000 row groups (bounded) and one of 16,386 whose matching
rows are in every other row group (keeps the estimate of the table
statistics), also when the row groups are transaction-local.

The tests assert the estimates directly. No existing test expectation
changes.

Note: this PR was generated by an AI coding agent.
subject: Bound a table scan's estimate by the rows of the row groups its filters cannot skip (#28793)

author: Mark <mark.raasveldt@gmail.com>
message:
A smaller alternative to duckdb/duckdb#28639. It fixes the same two v2.0
regressions after delim joins became materialized CTEs: a lateral UNNEST
runs out of memory, and a `json_valid` guard stops protecting a lateral
table function in a correlated subquery. It uses the same two planner
changes as duckdb/duckdb#28639 and leaves out the third.

**Kept from duckdb/duckdb#28639**
- `CanRestrictCorrelationDomain` now accepts `LOGICAL_UNNEST` and table
in-out functions that are not volatile and have no final step. The CTE
filter pusher can then move a guard on the outer rows into their input.
This alone fixes the Malformed JSON errors for `range`, `unnest` and
`json_each`.
- The rewrite no longer wraps its two CTEs in identity projections
(added in eb35d40269c for column pruning, which `RemoveUnusedColumns`
now handles for materialized CTEs). A filter that can throw therefore no
longer stops at a projection that isn't a query block boundary, and
reaches the UNNEST output. This fixes the OOM. duckdb/duckdb#28639 used
a projection flag for this instead.

**Left out**
- Running `EMPTY_RESULT_PULLUP` again after statistics propagation,
together with the anti-join projection-map change it needs. On main this
case already takes about 0.01 s (3M rows, the view example in
duckdb/duckdb#28639). The extra pass also changed which errors get
raised, and it forced edits to 4 unrelated tests (`deliminator.test`,
`scalar_aggregate_merge_tpcds_plan.test`, `test_window_self_join.test`,
`updating_the_join_node_hash_map_has_no_errors.test_slow`). None of
those tests change here.
- The two new test files are merged into one,
`test/sql/subquery/lateral/lateral_filter_into_delim_cte.test`, without
`PRAGMA enable_verification`. The file is skipped under
`verify_serializer` and `disable_optimizer`, as in duckdb/duckdb#28639,
because both drop the planner-only marks.

**Extra test**
- The new test also runs an `EXPLAIN` check that a wide table scanned
under a delim join CTE still projects only the columns it needs (`id,
pad1`), plus a result check on the same query. This confirms that
dropping the identity projections keeps column pruning.

**Results** (reldebug, before → after)

| query | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| lateral UNNEST + throwing filter, 4 GB limit | Out of Memory | 20 rows
counted, 0.34 s |
| `NOT EXISTS` + `json_valid` guard (range / unnest / json_each) |
Malformed JSON error | 2 |
| empty filter on view with lateral UNNEST, 3M rows | 0.012 s |
0.008–0.011 s |

Tests: the new test passes. `test/sql/subquery/*`, `test/optimizer/*`,
`test/sql/cte/*`, `test/sql/optimizer/*`, `test/sql/json/*` and
`test/sql/table_function/*` all pass (tpch/tpcds tests were skipped

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>

message:
Small fixes and additions to the stable C++ API (`tools/cpp`), found
while porting
[duckdb-odbc](https://github.com/Robinho-MR/duckdb-odbc/pull/1) from
DuckDB's internal C++ classes to `duckdb::cxx`. None of them changes the
C API or the engine.

### `StartupOptions::Set(name, value)`

`StartupOptions` only had five dedicated setters, while
`duckdb_v2_instance_create_with_options` accepts any option by name. So
the C++ API couldn't set any startup-only option that lacks a setter,
for example:
- `duckdb_api`, which every client sets to identify itself (the ODBC
driver sets `odbc`);
- `access_mode`;
- `extension_repository_directory`;
- any startup-only option a user puts in a connection string.

`Set` forwards a (name, value) pair to the C API, in the textual form
SQL `SET` accepts. Pairs are applied in the order given, after the
dedicated setters, so a later value wins. Options that need a running
instance (`allowed_directories`, ...) still go through
`Instance::GetConfig()`, as the C API documents.

### `Value::GetDecimal()` and a public `Value::CreateDecimal()`

`Value::Get<WIDTH, SCALE>()` and `Value::Create(decimal_t<WIDTH,
SCALE>)` need the width and scale at compile time. A driver learns them
at runtime, from a result column (`SQL_C_NUMERIC`) or a bound parameter
(`SQL_NUMERIC` with a precision and scale). Until now it couldn't read
the unscaled integer of a DECIMAL, nor create one, without going through
text.

- `Value::GetDecimal()` returns a `RuntimeDecimal {int128_t value;
uint8_t width; uint8_t scale;}`, through `duckdb_v2_value_get_decimal`.
- `Value::CreateDecimal(factory, int128_t value, width, scale)` was
already the private runtime forwarder of the typed constructor; it is
now public and documented.
- C API change: `duckdb_v2_value_create_decimal` now returns
`ERROR_INPUT_INVALID` for a value with more digits than the declared
width. Before, it only checked the storage tier, so e.g. 10000 at
`DECIMAL(4,0)` (or anything past 10^38 at width 38) built a value that
failed on bind or asserted in `ToText()`. INT16 and INT32 tier overflows
used to surface as an INTERNAL cast error; they are now
`ERROR_INPUT_INVALID` too.

### Compile when `<windows.h>` was included first

`<windows.h>` defines `DELETE` and `IGNORE` as macros. That turns the
`StatementType::DELETE` and `FunctionCollationHandling::IGNORE`
enumerators into syntax errors for any Windows consumer that includes it
before `duckdb_cpp.hpp`, which an ODBC driver must. The header now sets
both macros aside with `push_macro`/`pop_macro` while it is parsed.
These two are the only Windows macros among the header's enumerators.
Separately, `AddString` and `AddBlob` now call
`(std::numeric_limits<uint32_t>::max)()`, so the `max` macro (without
`NOMINMAX`) does not break them.

### Tests

New cases in `tools/cpp/tests` cover:
- startup-only options and aliases, override order, bad values and
unknown names;
- options that need a running instance;
- runtime DECIMALs across every storage tier, the typed constructor, a
query result, and out-of-range width, scale and value, plus non-DECIMAL
and NULL values.

`unittest "[cpp_api]"`: all 218 test cases pass (4248 assertions).
subject: C++ API: StartupOptions::Set, runtime DECIMAL access, windows.h compatibility (#28881)
title: C++ API: StartupOptions::Set, runtime DECIMAL access, windows.h compatibility

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
`SELECT DISTINCT` is often written defensively, or generated by a tool,
on top of something that cannot contain duplicates in the first place:
the columns include the primary key of the table, the input is a `GROUP
BY` on the same columns, a join against the key of a lookup table sits
in between, or the input of an `INTERSECT` / `EXCEPT` is itself a
`DISTINCT`. DuckDB plans every `DISTINCT` (and every `GROUP BY` without
aggregate functions) as a hash aggregate over all input rows, also when
the result is known to be the input.

This PR adds an optimizer, `redundant_distinct`, that removes such an
aggregate when its input provably has at most one row per value of the
group columns. The aggregate is replaced by a projection of the groups
under the same table index, so nothing above it has to be rebound. It
runs before join ordering.

The proof is structural, in a read-only helper (`Distinctness`):

* sources: the groups of an aggregate with a single grouping set, and
the `PRIMARY KEY` / `UNIQUE NOT NULL` constraints of a scanned table;
* these stay distinct through operators that never duplicate a row:
filters, limits, orderings, samples, windows, projections (plain column
references only), the left side of SEMI / ANTI / MARK / SINGLE joins,
and a side of an INNER join (the left side of a LEFT join) whose other
side is distinct on the columns of the join's equality conditions.

Statistics (distinct counts) are estimates and are never used.

`Distinctness` is the one place where unique column sets are inferred.
The inference that `ApplyFunctionalDependencies` had (scan constraints,
aggregates, projections, pass-through operators) moved into it;
`ApplyFunctionalDependencies` consumes it for its order key and window
simplifications, and
`ApplyFunctionalDependencies::GetUniqueColumnCombinations` remains as a
delegating entry point for its callers. The propagation through samples
and joins is in the helper as well and is enabled for
`redundant_distinct` only, so the existing consumers see the same unique
sets as before (their plans are unchanged). The unique sets of an
operator are computed once and cached per operator; an instance is valid
for the analysis of a stable plan and is not reused after a pass has
rewritten the operators it was asked about.

### Preconditions

The aggregate is removed only if

* it has no aggregate functions and no `GROUPING` functions, and one
grouping set that contains all groups;
* every group is a plain column reference;
* some set of columns that is proven distinct for the input is contained
in the groups.

Things that do not prove anything, each pinned by a test: a nullable
`UNIQUE` column (several NULLs are one group), part of a composite key,
an expression or cast of a key, a second grouping set, a LEFT join
against a side that is not distinct on the join key (and the
null-extended side of any outer join), an inequality or an expression as
the only join condition, an AsOf join, a cross product, a `UNION ALL`, a
table function.

`SET disabled_optimizers = 'redundant_distinct'` switches it off.

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, country INTEGER, segment INTEGER);
INSERT INTO customers SELECT i, i % 50, i % 7 FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE orders(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount INTEGER);
INSERT INTO orders SELECT i, (i * 7919) % 2000000, i % 97 FROM range(20000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE visits AS SELECT (i * 31) % 3000000 AS customer_id, i % 365 AS day FROM range(30000000) t(i);

SELECT DISTINCT o.id, o.amount FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE c.country < 25;
```

`orders.id` is a key, and the join against the key of `customers` does
not duplicate orders. Before:

```
AGGREGATE Groups: id, amount                                   ~8,803,200 rows
  COMPARISON_JOIN Join Type: INNER; Conditions: customer_id = id
    SEQ_SCAN orders
    SEQ_SCAN customers Filters: country < 25
```

After:

```
PROJECTION Expressions: id, amount
  COMPARISON_JOIN Join Type: INNER; Conditions: customer_id = id
    SEQ_SCAN orders
    SEQ_SCAN customers Filters: country < 25
```

User-mode instructions at one thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`,
median of 3, release build, `redundant_distinct` disabled vs. enabled in
the same binary; the queries are wrapped in `SELECT count(*) FROM
(...)`):

| query | disabled | enabled | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| the query above | 5.02e9 | 2.76e9 | 0.55 |
| `SELECT DISTINCT id, country, segment FROM customers` | 7.29e8 |
2.93e8 | 0.40 |
| `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM (SELECT customer_id, count(*) AS n
FROM visits GROUP BY customer_id) WHERE n > 5` | 3.76e9 | 3.28e9 | 0.87
|
| `SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM visits INTERSECT SELECT id FROM
customers WHERE country < 25` | 2.76e9 | 2.60e9 | 0.94 |

### Regression check

Disabled vs. enabled in the same binary on TPC-H and TPC-DS (SF1 and
SF10, with and without declared keys), JOB and ClickBench: the results
are identical at 1 and 32 threads (TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1, with and without
keys). Without declared keys 3 of the 121 TPC-H / TPC-DS plans change,
with declared keys 5; none in JOB or ClickBench. Instructions at one
thread on the changed plans are between 0.94x and 1.00x; no query is
slower than 1.05x.

### Tests

* `test/optimizer/redundant_distinct.test` (new): plan pins that the
aggregate is removed for each proof (GROUP BY key, `PRIMARY KEY`,
`UNIQUE NOT NULL`, composite key, through filter / sample / SINGLE join
/ INNER join, `INTERSECT` / `EXCEPT` of distinct inputs), that
`disabled_optimizers` brings it back, one negative pin per precondition
(the list above), and results: empty inputs, NULL keys, duplicates,
composite keys, `GROUPING SETS`, outer / AsOf / cross joins, DOUBLE
(NaN, -0.0), collations, nested types, and aggregates (including a
volatile one, `max(nextval(...))`) over a `DISTINCT` that has to stay.
* `test/optimizer/common_subplan.test_slow`: one query used `... FROM
(SELECT DISTINCT range FROM range(10)) GROUP BY range`, a GROUP BY on
the only column of a DISTINCT subquery. That GROUP BY is removed now,
which would leave two of the three nested common subplans the test is
about. The query groups by `range % 2` now (what its select list
computes); the expected plan is unchanged.
* `test/configs/verify_aggregate_state_export.json`: the new test is
added to the list of plan tests that are skipped in this configuration,
which rewrites the aggregates of every plan.

The tests in `test/optimizer`, `test/sql/join`, `test/sql/subquery`,
`test/sql/aggregate`, `test/sql/optimizer`, `test/sql/cte`,
`test/sql/setops`, `test/sql/sql_export` and the TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1
answer tests pass, `test/optimizer` and `test/sql/subquery` also with
`debug_verify_column_bindings` enabled.

Not part of this PR: removing a `DISTINCT` below an aggregate that
ignores duplicates (`max(x) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT ...)`). That is not
always a win, so it would need a cost decision.

#24971 and #24527 register an optimizer of the same name with a
different justification; they are complementary to the structural proof
used here.

This PR is independent of the other optimizer PRs I am opening next to
it (#28786, #28791); they add entries to `OptimizerType` and to the pass
list in `optimizer.cpp` as well, so they will conflict textually with
each other.

Note: this PR was generated by an AI coding agent.
subject: Remove DISTINCT / GROUP BY without aggregates over an input that is already distinct (#28792)

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
This PR fixes HTTP errors turning into JSON parse errors once the
per-host retry quota (#26947) refuses a retry. A failing httpfs read
then no longer reports the HTTP error, but `Serialization Error: Failed
to parse JSON string: {...}`, with the whole serialized HTTP error,
response headers included, as its message. For example, a range read
that keeps getting HTTP 429 from a rate-limited host fails this way
instead of with `HTTP 429 Too Many Requests`.

For requests that return their error instead of throwing
(`try_request`), `RunRequestWithRetry` keeps the error in
`request_error` and appends the quota exhaustion note to it. When the
request threw a DuckDB exception, or returned an error that holds one,
that string is the exception's JSON, so the note lands after the closing
brace. httpfs turns the request error back into an exception with
`ErrorData(response->GetRequestError())`, which parses anything that
starts with `{` as JSON and throws.

This PR appends the note to the exception message inside the JSON
instead, keeping the exception type and extra info, as the throwing path
already does. Plain text request errors get the note appended as before.

Could this get the `backport v2.0-cyanoptera` label? The retry quota is
in v2.0.0.
subject: Keep the HTTP error when the retry quota refuses a retry (#28920)
title: Keep the HTTP error when the retry quota refuses a retry

message:
Hi team, I found the following SQL weird
```sql
memory D COPY (SELECT 'a;b' AS s) TO '/tmp/nl_repro.csv' (NEW_LINE ';', HEADER false);
memory D SELECT content FROM read_text('/tmp/nl_repro.csv');
┌─────────┐

│ varchar │
├─────────┤
```

message:
A batched `COPY ... TO` given `ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES` without
`ROW_GROUP_SIZE` fails:

```sql
SET threads=2;
CREATE TABLE t AS FROM range(1000000);
COPY t TO 'out.csv' (ROW_GROUP_SIZE_BYTES '256KB');
-- INTERNAL Error: Attempting to get the index of an optional_idx that is not set
```

`CorrectSizeForBatch` calls `batch_size.GetIndex()` without checking
that a row target is set. It is
reached for the leftover batch of a non-final repartition, so the error
depends on timing: the
query above failed on every run at 2 threads here (tested on Linux
x86_64; Apple ARM64).

`CopyFunctionBatchAnalyzer::IsAcceptable()`,

author: Hannes Mühleisen <227792+hannes@users.noreply.github.com>
message:
Disclaimer: this PR is analyzed and completed by opus-5.5

Follow-up to https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28791, which added
`test/optimizer/pushdown/join_filter_pushdown_right_anti.test`. The test
fails in the **Vector Sizes** CI job, which builds with
`STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE=2`. That job is skipped in the merge queue, so the
failure only showed up after merge. It now fails on `main` and on every
open PR.

The two `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` checks at the end of the test expect the scan
of `big` to emit exactly 40 rows: the 40 rows with `k = 42`.
The join filter on `big` is `optional: k IN PRF(k)`. Like the other
optional runtime filters, it tracks its own selectivity over a window of
6 vectors and pauses itself when at least 50% of the rows pass.
- With 2048-row vectors the filter stays active and the scan emits
exactly 40 rows.
- With 2-row vectors the window is only 12 rows, so the filter pauses.
The row next to each matching row (`k = 45`) gets through, and the scan
emits 80 rows.

The query results are correct either way. Only the exact row count in
the plan changes.

message:
https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/12030

Ports prefix creation in ARTBuilder (CREATE INDEX) from the legacy
Prefix::New to PrefixHandle::New. The last prefix node now stays pinned
while the builder makes its child NodePtr point to the new leaf or inner
node.

PrefixHandle::New always allocates at least one prefix node, so the
builder only calls it if the keys share bytes before the next node.
Otherwise, the NodePtr above (the ART root, or a child of the parent
inner node) points directly to the leaf or inner node, as before.
Prefix::New loses its last caller and is removed.

The builder's stack still holds unpinned NodePtr references into parent
inner nodes; that is the next chunk.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
## Summary Enable adaptive min/max filtering of equality-join probe rows through shared machinery used by Parquet, native RLE, and DICT_FSST scans. The design separates two questions: - Does this value pass the filter? Cache that answer. - Is this optional filter saving work? Measure that from actual rows. Required predicates continue to apply when optional filters pause. ## Why this belongs in shared machinery A compressed entry can represent thousands of rows. Counting dictionary entries or runs therefore gives a different picture from counting actual rows. For example, two stored values might each appear once in a dictionary, while one represents almost every row. Evaluating the dictionary can suggest a useful filter even when it rejects almost nothing in practice. Native cached scans have this same problem as Parquet. They can also cache a temporary “accept everything” result when an adaptive filter is paused. Following the review feedback (https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28515#issuecomment-6821426694), this change replaces the Parquet-specific min/max matcher with shared cache support. ## Implementation The shared implementation provides three guarantees: 1. Pure mask construction. Evaluate the underlying predicate without advancing adaptive counters or recording a paused pass-through result. 2. Feedback from actual row batches. Cached and fallback paths update the same per-filter state. Paused filters still advance their retry clock. 3. Independent mandatory filtering. Keep mandatory and optional results separate, preserving required predicates and evaluation order when optional filters pause. Caches are invalidated when their owning filter state expires. Unsafe predicates, unsupported adaptive expressions, and native segments requiring separate NULL validity use the existing row-evaluation fallback. ## Performance There will be - Before the fix - Original PR with min-max adaptive filter - Then the current after follow comments of reviewer ## The measured tradeoff comparing with original PR Keeping cached answers adds machinery, so we compared it with both the original PR and the simpler row-evaluation fallback. The table below shows earlier selective native-storage fixtures. A millisecond (ms) is one thousandth of a second. Lower times are better. The shared cache was about 36–38% faster than fallback, while costing about 3% for RLE and 6% for the string dictionary versus the original PR. There is a counterexample to a universal speedup: skewed native RLE was 13.7% slower than fallback. These were small warm tests before the upstream merge: 737,280 rows, one thread, 18 measured queries per image and case. Timings were not repeated after that merge. Deprecated change - reference as bellow
Equality-join min/max fallback filters currently prune Parquet row groups - But do not reject individual probe rows when groups overlap the build range. Then - **Enable adaptive row** evaluation and **keep scalar comparisons** on the **fast executor path**. Parquet measures actual row rejection outside dictionary-mask evaluation, keeps cached predicates deterministic, and preserves periodic pause/resume so an unrepresentative prefix cannot disable filtering for the whole group. Predicates proved exactly `ALWAYS_TRUE` skip evaluation. The specialized path accepts direct scalar ranges; other expression shapes use the existing evaluator. Regression coverage includes - Selective filtering within overlapping groups, - Recovery after a matching prefix, - Dictionary row-frequency feedback, - Mandatory predicates, NULL semantics and native scans. Validation: - TDD: the baseline emits 180,000 probe rows for 18,060 join matches. - The selective scan, recovery and dictionary-feedback regressions pass with the implementation. - Saved validation records for the rebased tree show 34 SQL comparisons, 17 native checks, and 183 assertions across five focused sqllogictest files (51 assertions in the three new regression files). These are targeted results, not a full-suite claim. - Scoped formatting and `git diff --check` pass; the optional local spelling tool was unavailable. - [Fork PR and CI results](https://github.com/kevintruong/duckdb/pull/2). T ## Parent-versus-head performance evaluation Re-evaluated - Upstream parent `6145a8699b5e54b146fb305a862012b58130e9b8` - Against PR head `0b6d5a35edeb9c9bd6d76233dffc29ff9a985eb1` - Using matching macOS arm64 compiler flags: `-O3`, assertions enabled, sanitizers disabled. - -The saved head runtime reports pre-amend build ID `7cd49cc31c`; its evaluated source blobs were verified against the final PR head. | Workload | Grounded finding | |---|---| | Selective join | Approximately 65% faster, about 2.9× speedup | | Broad and redundant-broad | Approximately 1.8% more executed instructions | | 90%-match | Instruction count essentially unchanged | | Native broad-match | No consistent slowdown established | The runs use the original issue's - 30-million-row probe fixture - Identical SQL/settings - And paired runtime order. Selective speedup is the paired geometric-mean estimate at two threads: - Head/parent time ratio `0.346` (95% bootstrap interval `0.324–0.370`). - Probe output falls from 30 million to 3.01 million rows while all 245 row groups are still scanned; this is not an I/O reduction claim. Controls use order-entry thresholds of 14 minutes (broad), 2,100 minutes (approximately 90% match), and 18,900 minutes (selective), with redundant probe predicates `ol_o_id >= 2` or `ol_o_id >= 2700`. Timing batches include 8 paired rounds and an independent 12-round confirmation with an identical-head-binary control; native and single-thread controls are also included. All 399 workload executions matched count/SUM checks, including 300 unprofiled timed queries and 24 profiles. Profiled runs did not spill. Instruction measurements are whole-process counts at one thread, with five queries per native process, including startup/setup. - Observed changes were `+1.815%` for broad, - `+1.814%` for redundant-broad, - And `−0.065%` for the 90% control. - - These percentages describe executed work, not wall-clock regressions. Related to #28269. AI-assisted implementation and validation.
