message: This PR adds a new `LogicalType::GEOGRAPHY` # Motivation Since v1.5 we've had the `LogicalType::GEOMETRY` in core. `GEOMETRY` is used to represent different geometrical and geographic entities such as points, lines and polygons. However, almost all functions (and optimizations, such as stats computation) assume that `GEOMETRY` operates in cartesian _planar_ space. This makes it very easy and efficient to operate on and works great to represent geographic entities located relatively close to each other (e.g. within a medium-sized country), but becomes problematic once things are far enough apart that the curvature of the earths surface starts to become important. This has led many other systems and table/file formats to the introduce a separate `GEOGRAPHY` type, which explicitly should be interpreted as representing geographical entities _on a sphere_, not in _planar_ coordinates. Every "edge" between vertices in a `GEOGRAPHY` should therefore be considered "arcs" along a sphere, not just straight lines. Spatial has previously provided some support for spherical computation without introducing a new type by having separate functions that operate on `GEOMETRY`, such as `ST_Distance`/`ST_Distance_Sphere`. Representing these semantic concepts as separate types instead enables implementing separate overloads for the same geometric functions (such as e.g. `ST_DIstance`, `ST_Area`) that are specialized for these different use-cases. It also gives better type safety, as you cannot accidentally mixup geometries and geographies. But the primary reason we are interested in adding this type now is that it makes it easier for DuckDB to interact with other systems that have dedicated `GEOGRAPHY` types as we otherwise would require users to set some sort of `bool is_geography` flag on import/export, or do a silent conversion (like we do when reading geography from parquet) which is not great either. Given that `GEOGRAPHY` has been supported for a while already in both parquet and iceberg, the network effects are strong. # Changes ## New type The `LogicalTypeId::GEOGRAPHY` works almost the same as a `GEOMETRY`: it can hold an optional CRS, and is just a `PhysicalType::VARCHAR` underneath. A `GEOGRAPHY` value is therefore also essentially the same as a `GEOMETRY` value (they share the same internal representation), but its a bit more strict in what it considers a "valid" value. E.g. the vertices of a `GEOGRAPHY` is only allowed to be within X: -180 to +180 and Y: -90 to +90. This is checked on casts, conversion functions, and arrow import. - __Casts:__ - `GEOMETRY` and `GEOGRAPHY` can cast explicitly in both directions (no implicit casts) - `GEOGRAPHY` can also cast explicitly to/from `VARCHAR`/`BLOB` - A cast between explicit, different CRSs is rejected. - Untyped literals and `NULL` prefer the `GEOMETRY` overload of a function, so calls don't become ambiguous. - __Functions:__ - New function: `ST_GeogFromWKB` convert (and validate) a WKB blob to `GEOGRAPHY` - `ST_AsWKB` now accepts `GEOGRAPHY` too - `ST_AsBinary` now accepts `GEOGRAPHY` too - `ST_AsText` now accepts `GEOGRAPHY` too - `ST_AsWKT` now accepts `GEOGRAPHY` too - `ST_CRS` now accepts `GEOGRAPHY` too - `ST_SetCRS` now accepts, and keeps `GEOGRAPHY` type too - `vertex_extract` along with its `.x` field syntax, now accepts `GEOGRAPHY` too - `&&`/`ST_Intersects_Extent` now support `GEOGRAPHY` with geodetic semantics and row-group pruning. That said, most of these new overloads arebasically the same as the `GEOMETRY` variant internally, except for a small validation check. The only functions we have in core DuckDB that now actually operates significantly differently on `GEOMETRY`/`GEOGRAPHY` is the "extent" computation, which is used by both statistics collection/propagation and the `&&` intersection operator. ## Geodetic Coverage Extents For `GEOMETRY`, computing the extent (or bounding box) is easy: just accumulate the min/max of all vertices in a geometry (or a geometry column). For `GEOGRAPHY`, its significantly more complex, as we consider the extent of a `GEOGRAPHY` to be the extent of its _covering_, not just the _vertices_. Because the edges form arcs, they can "bulge" outwards towards the poles, in which case we need to include the "apex" of the bulge into the extent as well. The extent computations is generally where the majority of the complexity in this PR lies, everything else is pretty boilerplate. Another thing that adds to this complexity is that when dealing with `GEOGRAPHY` we have to consider how rings are oriented. When we compute the extent (or do other spatial operations) we generally need to know where the "interior" of a polygon. Any closed ring will divide the whole sphere into two regions, so which one do we compute the extent of? Figuring out which side is the inside gets particularly fun when a polygon stretches across an entire hemisphere. Our rule is **interior on the left**. This is the same convention as the S2 library uses (and what BigQuery does when passed `oriented => TRUE` on ingestion). For each polygon, the first non-empty ring is the shell, and when walking its vertices in order, the interior is on your left. Holes never add coverage, only their edges count. |Shell|Interior|Extent| |---|---|---| |Has a near-antipodal (ambiguous) edge|unknown|full globe| |Winds about +360° (eastward)|contains the north pole|full longitude, up to 90°N| |Winds about −360° (westward)|contains the south pole|full longitude, down to 90°S| |Doesn't wind, counterclockwise at its highest point|the bounded, pole-free side|the edges' extent| |Doesn't wind, clockwise|the complement|full globe| |Cusp, degenerate, touches a pole, or winds ≥ 540°|undefined|full globe| ## Serialization & Storage This PR adds a new `v2.1.0` (`70`) storage version, and serialization version `9`. We check for this when storing `GEOGRAPHY` columns and error when targeting older versions. Like mentioned above, the geometry shredding optimization is only enabled for single-point `GEOGRAPHY` columns. Everything else stays WKB, because per-ordinate stats can't represent wrapped or bulging extents. There's also a defensive widening in `InterpretStats` ## Interoperability - __Parquet writing:__ native Parquet `GEOGRAPHY` logical type with `algorithm=SPHERICAL` and CRS support, plus native geospatial statistics with a coverage bbox that may wrap. - __Parquet reading:__ Parquet `GEOGRAPHY` -> `GEOGRAPHY`, but we ignore the edge algorithm. A file's bbox is trusted as a coverage bound, wrapped bboxes are accepted, and out-of-range bboxes are ignored. GeoParquet edges set to anything non-planar now maps to `GEOGRAPHY` instead of throwing `NotImplementedException`. - __Arrow:__ `geoarrow.wkb` with `edges=spherical` <-> `GEOGRAPHY`. - __C API:__ `DUCKDB_TYPE_GEOGRAPHY = 43` (v1) and `LOGICAL_TYPE_ID_GEOGRAPHY = 61` (v2). The CRS getters accept `GEOGRAPHY`. - __JSON:__ treated like `GEOMETRY`. - __test_all_types:__ now includes `GEOGRAPHY`, which explains the many updated test expectations. ## Internals in `geometry.cpp` - I've added a shared `WKB` "visitor" class to make it easier to process WKB blobs, now that we need to process vertices differently when computing planar/geodetic extents. - I've added some geodetic math helpers: `Lonlat`/`Vec2`/`Vec3`, etc. These are in an internal namespace but could maybe be moved out if useful for others in the future. # Limitations & Future work - __Orientation convention:__ we consider the interior on the left. Alternatively we could add a "interior is the smaller region" mode like what BigQuery's uses as the default in the future. The major downside of our current approach is that clockwise data (shapefile/ESRI) gets full-globe extents, and any extension implementing `GEOGRAPHY` predicates has to use the same rule. - __Spherical edges only__: an ellipsoidal edge algorithm declared in a Parquet file/Arrow is ignored and read as spherical. I dont think these are that common in the wild, and I don't really think we want to implement support to handle all of these either for the foreseeable future, but I suppose we could warn or something instead. - __Parquet bbox semantics__: we write coverage bounds, which are wider than coordinate-based bbox and therefore safe for readers that don't expect this to be the case. However when reading we also assume the bbox represents the coverage bounds, and files whose writers stored coordinate-only bboxes for lines or polygons could prune incorrectly. This isn't really that well-defined in the spec, but I've been assured that this is the correct interpretation. There is not really a good way to know if a writer has written coverage bounds or coordinate bounds, so maybe we want to add some option or setting to control to this to guard against less sophisticated parquet writers in the future. - __Poles aren't identified as single points:__ `POINT(0 90)` and `POINT(90 90)` have disjoint extents. - __No geodetic predicates in core:__ only the bounding-box operator `&&`, we'll leave the rest for extensions. - __No PostGIS__ integration: we will have to update `pg_duckdb` and the `postgres_scanner` extensions separately. However IIRC postgres does not support geographical polygons covering more than a hemisphere, so we may need to do some additioanl conversion/checks there. - We need to figure out what to do with https://github.com/paleolimbot/duckdb-geography. It would be great if we could avoid breaking all the databases that have created a bunch of tables with `GEOGRAPHY` columns from the extension already. I think DuckDB should be able to tell these apart internally though, and by adding an implicit cast from the core to the extension type (and vice versa) the actual user-facing change may be pretty minimal. We may also improve/work on better support for extension namespacing soon too, but we will see. Will require further investigation.

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
## What this changes

`PartialAggregatePushdown` pre-aggregates the aggregate side of a join
by the join key when the query groups by columns of the other side (the
one-sided eager group-by). It does this for a plain `GROUP BY`, but
never for `GROUP BY ROLLUP (...)`, `CUBE (...)` or cascadable `GROUPING
SETS (...)` over the same join.

The reason is an interaction of two passes. The grouping sets optimizer
turns a ROLLUP into a cascade: the finest level aggregates the join and
exports its aggregate states (`EXPORT_STATE`), and every coarser level
combines the states of the level below it (`combine_aggr`).
`IsSupportedAggregate` rejects an aggregate that already exports its
state (2096a3d233f), because the pushdown would export it a second time
and finalize the result, which does not give back the type the cascade
expects. So the finest level, the only one that reads the join, is never
pushed.

This PR handles that case instead of rejecting it. For an aggregate that
already exports its state:

- the lower aggregate (below the join, grouped by the join key) is the
exported aggregate as it is. It is not exported a second time.
- the upper aggregate (above the join, the original groups) is
`combine_aggr(state)`, as for every other pushed aggregate.
- the final projection passes the combined state on instead of calling
`finalize`, because the consumers of the aggregate (the coarser levels
of the cascade) expect the state.

The finest level then looks like every other level of the cascade: it
combines states. The trigger is the existing one
(`PassesCardinalityHeuristic`, `PassesLowerGroupHeuristic`), and the
double-eager and owner-outer rewrites still refuse exported aggregates.

Two things come with it:

- An exported aggregate whose update or combine can throw is not pushed
below an inner join (see "When it fires").
- A hash aggregate of `combine_aggr` can now spill arena-backed states.
`AggregateStateSpilling::TryCreateSpillPlan` needs the state layout of
every aggregate, and `combine_aggr` has no state type of its own, so a
level that combines states (every coarser level of a cascade, and with
this PR the finest one) could not move its states to spillable storage
the way the aggregate that exported them can. The spill plan now takes
the layout of the aggregate whose states `combine_aggr` accumulates
(`ExportAggregateFunction::TryGetCombinedStateLayout`). `combine_aggr`
itself does not get a state type callback: that would make it
exportable, and the optimizer passes that look at
`HasGetStateTypeCallback` would start exporting it.

## Query shape

A grouped aggregate over a fact table joined to one or more dimension
tables, grouped by dimension columns with subtotals:

```sql
SELECT d.a, d.b, sum(f.x), avg(f.x), count(*)
FROM fact f JOIN dim d ON f.k = d.k
GROUP BY ROLLUP (d.a, d.b);
```

This is the usual form of a reporting query: totals per product, with
subtotals per brand and per category, and a grand total. The fact table
has many rows per join key, the groups are wide dimension attributes
(names, categories), and the aggregates are sums, counts, averages,
minima and maxima of fact columns. Without the pushdown every fact row
is joined to its dimension row and then hashed on the wide group
columns. With it, the fact rows are aggregated once on the integer join
key, and the join and the cascade above it only see one row per key.

It also applies to an aggregate that a query exports itself (`sum(x)
EXPORT_STATE` grouped by dimension columns over a join): the states are
combined above the join and returned without a `finalize`.

## When it fires

All preconditions of the one-sided pushdown apply unchanged. The
aggregate must

- sit directly on an INNER comparison join, or on a LEFT / RIGHT join
that preserves the aggregate side, with equality conditions whose
aggregate-side keys are column references;
- have no DISTINCT, FILTER or ORDER BY, at most one argument, and a
state type (`HasGetStateTypeCallback`);
- take its arguments from one side of the join only, and group by at
least one column of the other side, with more group columns than the
lower aggregate would have;
- have no argument that can throw below an inner join (#28573);
- new, for an aggregate that already exports its state: not be able to
throw in its update or combine below an inner join. The lower aggregate
also aggregates the rows the join removes, so `sum` / `avg` over HUGEINT
or DECIMAL(38), which add with an overflow check, could fail on rows the
query never aggregates. The check is the function's own error mode
(`FunctionErrors::CAN_THROW_RUNTIME_ERROR`, what
`BoundAggregateExpression::CanThrow` reads), not a list of types. As
with throwing arguments, a LEFT / RIGHT join that preserves the
aggregate side keeps every row anyway and is still pushed;
- pass the cardinality heuristic (the join keeps at least 70 % of the
aggregate side and that side is at least 4x the other side, or the join
expands).

The estimate of the new lower aggregate is capped as in #28716.

For a cascade, the grouping sets optimizer only exports aggregates that
are combinable and have no destructor, so the aggregates that reach the
pushdown this way are `sum`, `count`, `count(*)`, `avg`, `min`, `max`,
`any_value` / `first` / `last`, `bool_and` / `bool_or`, `bit_and` /
`bit_or` / `bit_xor`, `product` and `approx_count_distinct`. Below an
inner join the variants marked as able to throw stay above the join:
`sum` and `avg` over HUGEINT and DECIMAL(38), `skewness`, `kurtosis`.
DISTINCT and ordered aggregates are not part of a cascade and stay where
they are.

The plain `GROUP BY` path of the pass is not changed by this PR. It does
not have the new check, so `sum(HUGEINT)` grouped by dimension columns
over an inner join can still overflow on rows the join removes. That is
the behaviour on main and is tracked separately.

## Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE products AS
    SELECT i AS product_id, 'category ' || (i % 20) AS category, 'brand ' || (i % 5000) AS brand, 'product ' || i AS name
    FROM range(100000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE sales AS
    SELECT (i * 7919) % 100000 AS product_id, i % 100 AS quantity FROM range(20000000) t(i);

SELECT category, brand, name, sum(quantity), avg(quantity), count(*)
FROM sales JOIN products USING (product_id)
GROUP BY ROLLUP (category, brand, name);
```

| | 1 thread | 8 threads |
|---|---|---|
| main | 2.01 s | 0.27 s |
| this PR | 0.31 s | 0.08 s |

(Release build, arm64, best of 5 warm runs, on a shared machine. The
rows are identical.)

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` at 8 threads, finest level of the cascade only (the
coarser levels are the same in both plans).

main, 0.249 s:

```
HASH_GROUP_BY (rows=100000, time=0.65s) Groups: #0, #1, #2; Aggregates: sum(#3) EXPORT_STATE, count_star() EXPORT_STATE, count(#3) EXPORT_STATE
  PROJECTION (rows=20000000, time=0.00s) Projections: category, brand, name, quantity
    PROJECTION (rows=20000000, time=1.05s) Projections: #0, __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#1), __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#2), __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#3)
      HASH_JOIN (rows=20000000, time=0.08s) Join Type: INNER; Conditions: product_id = product_id
        TABLE_SCAN (rows=20000000, time=0.04s) Table: sales
        TABLE_SCAN (rows=100000, time=0.00s) Table: products
```

this PR, 0.071 s:

```
HASH_GROUP_BY (rows=100000, time=0.01s) Groups: #0, #1, #2; Aggregates: combine_aggr(#3), combine_aggr(#4), combine_aggr(#5), combine_aggr(#6)
  PROJECTION (rows=100000, time=0.00s) Projections: category, brand, name, #3, #4, #5, #6
    PROJECTION (rows=100000, time=0.00s) Projections: __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#0), __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#1), __internal_compress_string_uhugeint(#2), #3, #4, #5, #6
      HASH_JOIN (rows=100000, time=0.01s) Join Type: INNER; Conditions: product_id = #0
        TABLE_SCAN (rows=100000, time=0.00s) Table: products
        PROJECTION (rows=100000, time=0.00s)
          HASH_GROUP_BY (rows=100000, time=0.34s) Groups: #0; Aggregates: sum(#1) EXPORT_STATE, count_star() EXPORT_STATE, count(#1) EXPORT_STATE
            TABLE_SCAN (rows=20000000, time=0.04s) Table: sales
```

The 20M-row join, the string compression of the group columns and the
20M-row aggregate on three string columns are replaced by one 20M-row
aggregate on the integer join key. Everything above it handles 100k
rows.

## Relation to #28573 and #28716

Both apply to the new case without changes, because it goes through the
same code path:

- #28573: an exported aggregate whose argument can throw stays above an
inner join. `sum(CAST(s AS INTEGER))` under a ROLLUP is not pushed,
`sum(TRY_CAST(s AS INTEGER))` is (tested, with rows that only fail on
the fact rows the join drops).
- #28716: the lower aggregate created for an exported aggregate gets the
capped estimate (its input and the product of its group domains).

Float sums: as with the existing pushdown of a plain `GROUP BY`, the
states are combined in a different order than without the pushdown, so a
floating-point `sum` / `avg` can differ in the last digits. This is the
same reassociation the pass already does, and that parallel aggregation
does anyway.

## Tests

- `test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown_exported_state.test`
- plans: the pre-aggregate is below the join for ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING
SETS (with a fact column among the groups), with GROUPING() and HAVING
on top, for LEFT / RIGHT joins that preserve the aggregate side, for an
aggregate the query exports itself, and for every one-argument aggregate
function the cascade exports;
- plans that must not change: the pass disabled; no aggregate with an
argument (`count(*)` only); arguments from both sides; FILTER; two
arguments; DISTINCT; ordered aggregate; an argument that can throw below
an inner join (and its `TRY_CAST` twin that is pushed); an aggregate
that can throw below an inner join (and the LEFT JOIN twin that is
pushed); the aggregate side not preserved (`dim LEFT JOIN fact`, FULL
join); a non-equality join condition; an aggregate below the aggregate
side; no group from the other side; a single group column; a

threads: NULL join keys, NULL arguments, NULL group values next to the
NULLs of the ROLLUP, unmatched fact rows, a duplicated dimension key, an
empty dimension side, a fact side that is empty only at run time (so the

-
`test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown_exported_state_star_join.test`:
a ROLLUP over a fact table joined to a filtered dimension and to the

0.01). The pre-aggregate sits between the two joins; rows equal to the

`test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown_exported_state_overflow.test`:

`test/optimizer/partial_aggregate_pushdown_exported_state_external.test_slow`:

- Plans: TPC-H SF1 / SF10 (22 queries each), TPC-DS SF1 / SF10 (99

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
An anti join whose preserved side is small and whose other side is large
("accounts in this region that have no event", `small EXCEPT big`, an
`ANTI JOIN` against a fact table) is flipped by the build side optimizer
into a RIGHT ANTI join: the small side is built, the large side probes.
The probe rows of a RIGHT ANTI join are never emitted, they only mark
build rows as matched, and the join returns the build rows that were not
marked. A probe row whose key does not occur on the build side cannot
mark anything, so it does not have to reach the join at all. That is
exactly the situation join filter pushdown exists for, and it already
handles RIGHT SEMI joins this way, but
`JoinFilterPushdownUtil::JoinTypeIsSupported` rejected RIGHT ANTI
together with ANTI ("FIXME: anti/right_anti - we could do this, but need
to invert the join conditions"). The inversion is only needed for a
plain ANTI join, whose unmatched probe rows are the result. For RIGHT
ANTI the build keys can be pushed into the probe side as they are.

This PR makes RIGHT ANTI a supported join type of join filter pushdown:

`JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN` generates the filters (min/max, IN list, bloom
filter, as for any other join) for RIGHT ANTI comparison joins,
including the filters that are pushed into a materialized CTE on the
probe side.

With several equality keys the join gets the per-column bloom or
prefix-range filters of #28726 under the same condition as any other
join (build side at most 5% of the estimated probe side), and a scan
that #28768 lets wait for a small filter producer waits for a RIGHT ANTI
join as it does for a RIGHT SEMI join.

Plain ANTI joins stay unsupported. The choice of the build side is not
changed: `BUILD_SIDE_PROBE_SIDE` does not give RIGHT ANTI the dynamic
filter bonus it gives RIGHT SEMI. An ANTI join with a small filtered
preserved side is flipped by the size comparison already, and I found no
case in which the bonus alone decides the orientation (it needs a
preserved side that is at least 64 times smaller in rows than the scan
on the other side and still more expensive to build). Nothing changes in
the executor: the hash join already publishes its filters independently
of the join type.

### Preconditions

* the join is a RIGHT ANTI comparison join (i.e. an ANTI join that the
build side optimizer flipped);
* everything `JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN` requires for the other join types:
the probe-side key expressions are not volatile, and the filter is only
pushed through operators and into scans that accept it.

The filters are part of `JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN`: `SET disabled_optimizers
= 'join_filter_pushdown'` disables them together with all other join
filters.

### Example

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts AS SELECT i AS id, i % 50 AS region, i % 7 AS tier FROM range(2000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE events AS SELECT (i * 31) % 3000000 AS account_id, i % 365 AS day, i % 97 AS amount FROM range(60000000) t(i);

SELECT count(*) FROM accounts a ANTI JOIN events e ON a.id = e.account_id WHERE a.region = 7 AND a.tier = 3;
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, before:

```
HASH_JOIN    Join Type: RIGHT_ANTI; Conditions: account_id = id
  TABLE_SCAN events    Projections: account_id                                             60,000,000 rows
  TABLE_SCAN accounts  Filters: region = 7, tier = 3                                            5,714 rows
```

After:

```
HASH_JOIN    Join Type: RIGHT_ANTI; Conditions: account_id = id
  TABLE_SCAN events    Projections: account_id; Dynamic Filters: optional: account_id IN PRF(id)  114,280 rows
  TABLE_SCAN accounts  Filters: region = 7, tier = 3                                               5,714 rows
```

User-mode instructions at one thread (`perf stat -e instructions:u`,
median of 3, release build, `main` vs. this PR):

| query | main | this PR | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ANTI JOIN` (above) | 3.19e9 | 2.14e9 | 0.67 |
| `SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE region = 7 AND tier = 3 EXCEPT SELECT
account_id FROM events` | 3.18e9 | 2.13e9 | 0.67 |

A `NOT EXISTS` over the same tables does not change: it is decorrelated
into a different plan that already restricts the scan of `events`.

### Regression check

Without vs. with the change on TPC-H and TPC-DS (SF1 and SF10), JOB and
ClickBench: the results are identical at 1 and 32 threads (TPC-H /
TPC-DS SF1), and no `EXPLAIN` plan changes (join filters are not part of
the plan text, and no join changes sides). 3 of the 121 TPC-H / TPC-DS
queries have a RIGHT ANTI join; their instructions at one thread are
between 0.97x and 1.02x. There is none in JOB or ClickBench.

### Tests

`test/optimizer/pushdown/join_filter_pushdown_right_anti.test` (new):
`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` pins that the probe scan of a RIGHT ANTI join gets
`Dynamic Filters` (also next to an inequality between the two sides),
that a plain ANTI join, a volatile probe key and `disabled_optimizers =
'join_filter_pushdown'` give none, and results for NULL keys on either
side with `=` and `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, `NOT IN`, duplicate build
keys, two equality keys, VARCHAR keys, an empty probe side, an empty
build side, an anti join below an outer join, over an aggregate, over a
materialized CTE (one consumer, two anti join consumers whose filters
are combined, and an anti join next to an unfiltered consumer),
`EXCEPT`, and inside a recursive CTE. For joins on several keys it pins
the per-column filters (the same as for the RIGHT SEMI join, min/max
only above the 5% bound) and the results with NULLs in either key column
on both sides for `=`, `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` and a mix of the two, and
that a scan below an aggregate on the probe side waits for the filter
and the query still completes with an empty build side.

No existing expected plan changes. The tests in `test/optimizer`,
`test/sql/join`, `test/sql/subquery`, `test/sql/aggregate`,
`test/sql/optimizer`, `test/sql/cte`, `test/sql/setops`,
`test/sql/sql_export` and the TPC-H / TPC-DS SF1 answer tests pass,
`test/optimizer` and `test/sql/subquery` also with
`debug_verify_column_bindings` enabled.

#28732 converts more `NOT EXISTS` / `NOT IN` joins into ANTI joins
before join ordering, which produces more RIGHT ANTI joins for this
change to act on.

This PR is independent of the other optimizer PRs I am opening next to
it (#28786).

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Hi team, I notice reading from hive partitioned parquets doesn't always
get the correct type; for example
```sql
memory D COPY (
             SELECT TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 12:30:00' AS ts, TIME '12:30:00' AS t, DATE '2024-01-01' AS d, 1 AS v
         ) TO '/tmp/hive_repro' (FORMAT parquet, PARTITION_BY (ts, t, d));
memory D SELECT typeof(ts), typeof(t), typeof(d)
         FROM read_parquet('/tmp/hive_repro/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true);
┌────────────┬───────────┬───────────┐
│ typeof(ts) │ typeof(t) │ typeof(d) │
│  varchar   │  varchar  │  varchar  │
├────────────┼───────────┼───────────┤
│ VARCHAR    │ VARCHAR   │ DATE      │
└────────────┴───────────┴───────────┘
```
I think the root cause is
- Hive partition type detection cast the raw, URL-encoded directory
value, so TIMESTAMP partitions written by DuckDB were read back as
VARCHAR
- Detection now unescapes the value before trying the candidate casts,
as In the
[`HivePartitioning::GetValue`](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/blob/b54bafed481c85bf170006a30004c60394eeab80/src/common/hive_partitioning.cpp#L171)
already does when reading
subject: Detect hive partition types from unescaped values (#28885)

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
Fixes #28777

### Problem

For a DECIMAL with width = scale and width > 15, `to_json` and `CAST(...
AS JSON)` produce an invalid JSON number without a leading zero:

```sql
SELECT to_json('0.5'::DECIMAL(18,18));
-- before: .500000000000000000   (json_valid = false, cannot be read back)
-- after:  0.500000000000000000
```

Decimals wider than 15 digits are converted to VARCHAR and inserted as
raw JSON numbers. The VARCHAR form of a DECIMAL(w,w) has no integer part
(`.5`, `-.5`), which is not valid JSON.

### Fix

In the DECIMAL case of `CreateValues` in `json_create.cpp`, when width =
scale, the new helper `CreateRawDecimalValues` inserts a `0` before the
decimal point (`.5` -> `0.5`, `-.5` -> `-0.5`) before creating the raw
value. All other decimals take the existing path unchanged.

`to_json` and the `ANY -> JSON` cast share this code, so both are fixed,
including values inside lists, structs, and maps.

Not changed:
- The VARCHAR form of DECIMAL(w,w) stays `.5` (as checked in
`test/sql/types/decimal/test_decimal.test`). The fix is local to JSON
creation.
- Decimals with width <= 15 (written as DOUBLE) and decimals with
integer digits.

### Tests

New `test/sql/json/scalar/test_json_decimal_no_integer_digits.test`:
- `to_json` and `::JSON` for widths 16, 18, 19 and 38 (every physical
type)
- negative values, zero, the smallest and largest values, and NULL
- `json_valid` and reading the output back with `json_extract`
- nested lists, structs and maps, and column input
- unchanged output for `DECIMAL(19,18)`, `DECIMAL(18,2)`, `DECIMAL(3,3)`
and the VARCHAR cast

Locally (Linux aarch64, release build):
- the new test fails without the fix and passes with it, also with
`test/configs/warnings_as_errors.json`
- `test/sql/json/*` and `test/sql/types/decimal/*` pass
- `make format-check` passes
subject: Write the leading zero for DECIMAL values without integer digits in to_json and JSON casts (#28778)

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
hunk_contexts: enum class DeferredRuntimeFilterType : uint8_t { BLOOM_FILTER, PREFIX_RANGE };
message:
## Problem

`JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseInFilter` compares `ht->Count()` (the
number of build-side **rows**) against `dynamic_or_filter_threshold`.
The setting's description is "the maximum amount of OR filters", and
`PushInFilter` already deduplicates the values, so the limit is really
about **distinct values per key column**.

This hurts multi-column joins where one column has few distinct values.
For example, a MERGE / semi join on `(id, partition_key)`:

- 100 build rows covering 17 distinct `partition_key` values get no IN
filter on any column, because 100 > 50.
- The probe scan only gets a min/max range on `partition_key`. With
UUID-like keys that range covers nearly everything, so partitioned scans
(e.g. Iceberg identity partitions) prune almost nothing.

Against a `project_id`-partitioned Iceberg table, the number of data
files read jumped from 434 to 1,586 when the build side went from 50 to
51 rows (13 → 14 distinct partition values).

## Minimal Code to Reproduce

```sql
SET disabled_optimizers = 'join_order,build_side_probe_side';
CREATE TABLE probe AS SELECT ((i // 1000) * 1000003)::BIGINT AS grp, i::BIGINT AS id FROM range(1000000) t(i);
CREATE TABLE b AS SELECT ([0, 500, 999][(i % 3) + 1] * 1000003)::BIGINT AS grp,
                         ([0, 500, 999][(i % 3) + 1] * 1000 + i)::BIGINT AS id FROM range(200) t(i);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT count(*) FROM probe p JOIN b ON p.grp = b.grp AND p.id = b.id;
-- only `grp >= 0 AND grp <= 999002997`, although grp has 3 distinct values
```

## How we found it

We were benchmarking a periodic upsert `MERGE INTO` against an Iceberg
table (duckdb-iceberg, and AWS S3 Tables) partitioned by
`identity(project_id)`. The MERGE joins `ON target.id = source.id AND
target.project_id = source.project_id`. Batches are a few hundred rows
that touch 10–20 projects.

## Change

- `CanUseInFilter` now lets build sides of up to
`max(dynamic_or_filter_threshold, 65536)` rows try an IN filter. The
65536 cap bounds the cost of scanning the key column. A threshold of 0
or 1 still disables IN filters.
- `PushInFilter` stops deduplicating as soon as a column has more
distinct values than the threshold, and returns `false`. The caller then
falls back to the existing min/max filter, so behaviour for
high-cardinality keys is unchanged.

Feedback welcome.  Heavy LLM, needs review.
subject: Apply the dynamic IN filter threshold to distinct key values, not build rows (#28106)

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
Follow-up to #28787. The merge queue merged #28787 at its earlier head,
so the fixes for the last duckdb-bot review round did not land. This
applies them on top of main.

- `RESET profiling_renderer_settings` no longer validates. `{}` is
always valid, and RESET is the way out when the stored values do not fit
the active renderer.
- `SET profiling_renderer_settings` validates only the new values. It no
longer configures the renderer from the stored settings first, so a
stored bad value cannot block a valid SET. The new
`TreeRenderer::CreateRenderer(context, name, settings)` overload
configures a built-in renderer from the given settings.
- The setting stays local-only. Without a client context (a `DBConfig`
or `duckdb_set_config`), it throws `Could not set option
"profiling_renderer_settings" as a global option`, as the progress bar
settings do. Before #28787 it was rejected there; with #28787 it was
stored database-wide without validation, so a bad value broke `EXPLAIN`
in every connection.
- Removes the unused `client_config.hpp` include from
`tree_renderer.cpp` and `shell_profiler_renderer.cpp`.

Tests: `generic_migrated_settings.test` covers RESET and a valid SET
after an invalid value was stored. `test_config.cpp` covers the rejected
startup option. Locally (reldebug), the `test/sql/settings`,
`test/sql/pragma/profiling` and `test/sql/explain` suites pass, as do

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
A GET with a content handler streams its content and the handler can
stop the transfer at a size of its choosing, which is how the repository
metadata fetch caps itself at 64 KiB. The body of an error response
(status 400 and up) is not streamed but buffered for the error message,
and nothing bounded that buffer: a large 404 or 500 body was read whole
before the caller saw anything. Carried as patch 0004 until
duckdb-httpfs takes it: both backends keep only the first 64 KiB of such
a body.
subject: httpfs: cap the buffered body of an error response when the content is streamed (#28877)

message:
Follow-up to #28508, which added the failing-malloc shell tests
(`tools/shell/tests/test_malloc_failure.py`). Sweeping the byte budget
of that shim over every allocation boundary of a `SELECT 42` run,
instead of the handful of fractions the test uses, found three ways an
allocation failure still ends the process instead of surfacing as an
out-of-memory error.

## Problem

**A. Teardown skips the task drain (SIGSEGV).**
`ClientContext::~ClientContext` calls `Destroy()`, which took the
context lock through `LockContext()`, a heap allocation. After a query
fails with out-of-memory, that allocation fails too, the `catch (...)`
of the destructor swallows it and `CleanupInternal` never runs: the
active query and its `Executor` are destroyed while a worker thread is
still executing one of its tasks, and `Executor::PushTaskError` then
writes into the freed context.

**B. A worker's first setting lookup registers a `thread_local`
destructor (SIGABRT).** `GlobalUserSettings::GetSettings()` keeps a
`thread_local CachedGlobalSettings` with a non-trivial destructor. The
first time a worker thread reads a setting (`TaskScheduler::ProcessTask`
reads `scheduler_process_partial` before it runs its first task), the
C++ runtime registers that destructor with `__cxa_thread_atexit`, glibc
allocates the registration with `calloc`, and when that fails glibc
calls `__libc_fatal("failed to register TLS destructor: out of
memory")`, which no `catch` can see.

**C. Self-deadlock while scheduling the first tasks (hang).**
`Executor::InitializeInternal` held `executor_lock` across
`ScheduleEvents`, so the `PipelineInitializeTask`s of the initial
schedule were created and enqueued under that lock. When
`tasks.push_back(...)` or the enqueue failed to allocate after the task
was constructed, the task was destroyed, `~ExecutorTask` called
`Executor::UnregisterTask`, which locks `executor_lock`, and the query
thread waited for itself forever.

## Fix

* **A.** `ClientContext::Destroy()` constructs the `ClientContextLock`
on the stack, so taking the lock cannot fail; `CleanupInternal` then
drains the tasks of the active query before anything that still
allocates can throw. The remaining `catch (...)` in the destructor
covers the allocations of ending the query. `QueryResult::Close()`,
which `~QueryResult` runs, keeps its heap-allocated lock on purpose: a
result can be destroyed while the same thread already holds the context
lock (inside `ClientContext::Query` on the error path), where a stack
lock deadlocks and the failing allocation is what lets the destructor
return today.
* **B.** A worker thread now owns the two caches it reads under memory
pressure: `TaskScheduler::ExecuteForever` keeps a `WorkerSettingsCache`
and a `BlockAllocatorWorkerState` on its stack, and
`GlobalUserSettings::GetSettings()` /
`GetBlockAllocatorThreadLocalState()` use them while they exist, through
a plain `thread_local` pointer that needs no destructor. A worker
therefore never touches the `thread_local` objects and nothing is
registered with `__cxa_thread_atexit` on a worker. The block cache
allocates when it is created, so it is created inside the existing retry
loop of the worker, next to its consumer token: a thread that cannot
allocate it yet keeps retrying and takes no task until it has one. API
threads keep the `thread_local` caches and their destructors exactly as
before (their first setting read is at connection creation, long before
a query can exhaust the heap), so there is no leak and no change for
them. The block allocator part was exposed by the settings part: on
`main` the settings cache is always the first registration on a worker,
and once it was gone the sweep aborted in `BlockAllocator::AllocateData`
instead. Two alternatives were rejected: reading a setting when the
worker starts, which only moves the fatal registration to thread
creation and made the `0.25` startup budget and the `RLIMIT_AS` tests
abort; and a leaked per-thread heap cache, which grows without bound in
a process that churns API threads.
* **C.** `ScheduleEventsInternal` now only creates the events and
collects the ones without dependencies; `InitializeInternal` schedules
those after it released `executor_lock` (`ScheduleReadyEvents`). No task
of the executor exists before that point, so nothing can touch the
executor's `events` concurrently while they are built under the lock,
and the tasks created by scheduling can be destroyed on failure without
re-entering the lock. `CancelTasks` already destroys tasks outside the
lock for the same reason.

## Verification

All runs use the shim of `test_malloc_failure.py` on a release build
(`SELECT 42` through the shell, Linux aarch64, 192 hardware threads),
with the budget set to every allocation boundary in the last 10% of the
startup bytes ("exact sweep"), and to budgets jittered around the point
where the first tasks are scheduled and around the budgets of the `0.9`
and `0.98` test fractions ("jittered", 60 s timeout counts as a hang).
The comparison binary is `main` at c33123c88ab, the branch binary is
this PR on c8ef5ee51f9.

| run | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| exact sweep | 23324 runs: 2 SIGABRT (glibc TLS destructor), 1 hang |
23747 runs: 0 SIGSEGV, 0 SIGABRT, 0 hangs |
| jittered, 3000 runs around the first scheduling | 6 SIGSEGV
(`PushTaskError` on the freed context), 15 SIGABRT | 0 |
| jittered, 1500 runs wider band + 1600 runs around the 0.9 and 0.98
fractions | 13 SIGABRT, 1 hang (1500 runs) | 0 |

* `python3 -m pytest tools/shell/tests/test_malloc_failure.py
tools/shell/tests/test_address_space_limit.py --shell-binary
build/release/duckdb`: 21 passed, repeated 6 times.
* `build/release/test/unittest` for `test/sql/parallelism/*`,
`test/sql/settings/*` and `[api]`: all pass.
* `tools/shell/tests`: 655 passed; the 8 `.schema` tests fail because
this build has no `autocomplete` extension, unrelated.

No new test: the holes depend on which allocation fails first, which the
byte budget of the shim cannot select deterministically once worker
threads allocate concurrently, so the existing `test_malloc_failure.py`
and `test_address_space_limit.py` tests (which pass on this branch) plus
the sweep above are the coverage.

subject: Keep teardown and task scheduling safe when an allocation fails (#28656)

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
An insert large enough to write its row groups to disk before it commits
leaked those blocks when it committed while a concurrent checkpoint ran
and the WAL was replayed (after a crash, or a close without checkpoint)
before the next checkpoint: the blocks were counted as used twice and
were never freed again, even after the rows were deleted or the table
dropped. The database file kept the space and nothing reported it except
debug_verify_blocks ("Block 12 was used 7 times, but multi_use_blocks
says it is used 14 times"). No data was lost or read wrongly.

Such a commit logs the block pointers of its row groups to the WAL and
marks the blocks as checkpointed, so the next header lists them as used.
When the commit happens after a concurrent checkpoint's bound but before
its header, that checkpoint does not write the row groups, but its
header lists their blocks as used, with their multi-use counts. WAL
replay then marks the same blocks as used once more.

Newly used blocks now carry the commit that made them part of committed
storage. Flushing a commit stamps the blocks of its optimistically
written row groups with its commit id, and a header lists a newly used
block as used only if the checkpoint's bound is past that commit. A
checkpoint that started before the commit therefore lists the blocks as
free, WAL replay takes them from the free list, and the next checkpoint
includes them. A commit that rewrites one of its optimistically written
row groups, as after an ALTER in the same transaction, no longer marks
the unchanged columns' blocks as checkpointed before the commit either.

A commit that fails before its WAL flush leaves its blocks unstamped, so
its revert now returns them to the free list right away; previously they
waited for the next checkpoint.
subject: Do not leak the blocks of bulk inserts committed during a checkpoint (#26452)

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
Two small table changes:

- **Default extensions.** `glue` and `legacy_parser` are built and
distributed with every release (`core.cmake`, `cloud.cmake`) but were
missing from the default extension table in `extension_helper.cpp`, so
`duckdb_extensions()` did not list them until installed.
- **Autoload.** glue's functions, settings and external-resource types
were already in the autoload tables of `extension_entries.hpp`, but
`CanAutoloadExtension` refused the extension itself because it was not
in `AUTOLOADABLE_EXTENSIONS`. Added there and in
`scripts/generate_extensions_function.py`, which generates the header.

The second commit is separable if autoloading glue is not wanted yet.
subject: List glue and legacy_parser among the default extensions, let glue autoload (#28820)

message:
Builds on #26932 (BIGNUM `*`, `//`, `%`), #28263 (decimal width and
scale as `uint32_t`, with the glue and iceberg extension patches),
#28270 (`TableIndexList::Bind` resets the bind state when binding
throws), #28275 (join-condition verification statistics may not claim
NOT NULL after an earlier condition), #28276 (decimal rounding beyond
the width keeps NULLs) and #28258 (zstd allocation failure in the ICU
time zone loader reported as out of memory), all of which have merged.

This PR lifts the `DECIMAL` width limit of 38 digits. A `DECIMAL(width,
scale)` with `width > 38` stores its unscaled value as a BIGNUM blob
(`PhysicalType::VARCHAR`, C++ type `bignum_t`), while decimals up to 38
digits keep their fixed-size integer storage and all of their current
behaviour. The width is a `uint32_t`; a session binds widths up to the
`max_decimal_width` setting (default 1,000,000 digits), which bounds the
time and memory a single value can take.

```sql
SELECT 123456789012345678901234567890123456789012345.678 * 2.5 AS r, typeof(r);
-- 308641972530864197253086419725308641972530864.1950   DECIMAL(50,4)

CREATE TABLE t(d DECIMAL(60,2));
INSERT INTO t VALUES (999912345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567890.99), (-1.5);
SELECT sum(d), min(d), typeof(sum(d)) FROM t;
-- 999912345678901234567890123456789012345678901234567889.49   -1.50   DECIMAL(80,2)

SELECT typeof(repeat('9', 300)::DECIMAL(300,0) * repeat('9', 300)::DECIMAL(300,0));
-- DECIMAL(600,0)

-- BigQuery BIGDECIMAL(77,38) columns are now read exactly instead of as DOUBLE
SELECT * FROM 'data/parquet-testing/bigdecimal.parquet';
-- 578960446186580977117854925043439539266.34992332820282019728792003956564819967 ...
```

### Design

* **A fifth decimal tier, not a parallel code path.** Everywhere the
decimal code switches on the physical type (`INT16`, `INT32`, `INT64`,
`INT128`), the wide representation is the fifth case
(`PhysicalType::VARCHAR` with `bignum_t`): `Value::DECIMAL(bignum_t,
width, scale)` next to the `int64_t`/`hugeint_t` overloads,
`TryCastToDecimal`/`TryCastFromDecimal` specialisations for `bignum_t`
dispatched by the existing switches in `decimal_cast.cpp`, `bignum_t`
overloads of the arithmetic operators, bignum callbacks for
`round`/`ceil`/`floor`/`trunc`, a bignum tier for window `FILL`, and
`BignumIntermediate`-based kernels as the bodies of those
specialisations. The helpers in
`src/common/types/bignum_decimal.{hpp,cpp}` (powers of ten, rescaling
with rounding, parsing, formatting, double and two's complement
conversion) play the role `Hugeint::*` plays for the 128-bit tier.
* **The width is bounded by a setting, not by the representation.**
`Decimal::IsValidWidthScale` only requires a width of at least 1 and a
scale within the width, the `DECIMAL(width, scale)` type constructor
takes `UINTEGER` modifiers, and every existing use that meant "widest
fixed-size decimal" is `Decimal::MAX_WIDTH_INT128` (38), with
`Decimal::IsWide(width)` telling the tiers apart. The cost of a wide
value follows its declared width, so the session setting
`max_decimal_width` (default `Decimal::DEFAULT_MAX_WIDTH`, 1,000,000
digits; values below 38 act as 38) bounds every DECIMAL a session
constructs: a type modifier, a cast target, an arithmetic, `sum` or
`round` result or a common type beyond it raises an error that names the
setting (`Decimal::MaxWidth`, `Decimal::CheckedWidth`), and a literal
beyond it raises the same error (it never binds to another type, so a
stored view fails instead of changing its result when the setting is
lowered). The setting bounds the types a query constructs, not the types
it already has: a column written under a larger bound still reads,
compares, combines (`COALESCE`, `CASE`, `UNION`, joins) and aggregates
within its own width (`Decimal::CheckedWidth` checks a result against
the widest input as well as the setting), only a result wider than every
input is refused. `SET max_decimal_width = 38` restores the result-type
rules of the fixed-size tiers. The powers of ten of the bignum tier are
computed by binary exponentiation on the BIGNUM (the first 512 are
cached and read without locking, wider ones live in a cache bounded to
16 MB), BIGNUM magnitudes multiply with Karatsuba above 48 limbs,
decimal strings are parsed and printed by divide and conquer, and
`FitsWidth` decides by bit length, so a power is only ever built for a
value of about the width itself. Multiplication, division, rescaling,
parsing and printing check for interrupts
(`ClientContext::InterruptCheck`) about once a millisecond through the
`BignumArithmeticState`; the casts of the wide tier carry the context in
a `WideDecimalCastState`, so `Ctrl-C` and `max_execution_time` stop a
long conversion. `DecimalTypeInfo` serializes width and scale as LEB128
varints as before, so the storage format is unchanged.
* **Storage version.** Wide `DECIMAL` columns (including generated
columns), type aliases, macro parameter and return types, macro defaults
and the argument types recorded in exported aggregate states require
storage version 2.1.0 (`Decimal::WIDE_VERSION_ADDED`); a database at an
older storage version refuses them with a clear error, as VARIANT did
before 1.5.0. Below storage version 2.0.0 a `CAST` stores its target as
a `LogicalType`, so the stored expressions of views, macros, table
defaults, generated columns and CHECK constraints are walked and a cast
to a wide decimal is refused there too. In databases written before wide
decimals, expression-index keys and macro defaults are bound with the
result-type rules of those versions (`LegacyDecimalResultTypeScope`), so
a persisted `UNIQUE INDEX ON t((a * b))` over `DECIMAL(38,2)` columns
keeps the `DECIMAL(38,4)` keys older versions wrote and read, and a
default `x := 1::DECIMAL(38,0) * 1::DECIMAL(38,0)` folds to the
`DECIMAL(38,0)` those engines bind (the index keys verified against the
released 1.5.6 and 2.0.0 binaries, the macro defaults, views and
aggregate states against 2.0.0).
* **Representation.** The BIGNUM encoding is order-preserving under
`memcmp`, so comparisons, `ORDER BY`, `MIN`/`MAX`, `DISTINCT`, hashing,
joins, sort keys and ART indexes work on wide decimals without
decimal-specific code. The scale lives in the type, as before.
* **Statistics.** Wide decimal columns carry `BignumStats`, a statistics
kind modelled on `GeometryStats` that holds the exact minimum and
maximum as BIGNUM blobs (variable length, no truncation). It plugs into
the same places as `NumericStats`: zonemap checks for comparisons, `IN`
and `BETWEEN`, the statistics propagator (filters, comparisons, casts,
`min`/`max`, and exact bounds for `+`, `-`, `*`), the `ORDER BY ...
LIMIT` row-group reorderer and the Parquet reader's statistics. The
BIGNUM type itself keeps its current string statistics, since changing
its kind would alter the statistics stored for existing BIGNUM columns.
* **Results keep their exact width.** Arithmetic (`+`, `-`, `*`, `%`),
comparisons and type combination (`UNION`, `COALESCE`, `CASE`, `VALUES`,
...) grow past 38 digits whenever the result needs it, and keep growing:
`DECIMAL(38,2) + DECIMAL(38,2)` is `DECIMAL(39,2)`, `DECIMAL(38,2) *
DECIMAL(38,2)` an exact `DECIMAL(76,4)` and `DECIMAL(300,0) *
DECIMAL(300,0)` an exact `DECIMAL(600,0)`, where main clamps to 38
digits and raises an overflow error at run time (or, for type
combination, silently truncates the scale). Since no wide result is
clamped, the wide tier has no overflow-checking kernels; the bounds are
`max_decimal_width` and the `uint32_t` range of the width, reported at
bind time by `Decimal::CheckedWidth` ("Multiplication needs a DECIMAL of
120 digits, the maximum DECIMAL width is 100 (SET max_decimal_width to
allow wider decimals)"). Type combination (`COALESCE`, `CASE`, `VALUES`,
`UNION`) raises the same error for a wide result beyond the bound
instead of truncating its scale. Results that fit in 38 digits keep
their fixed-size representation and kernels, and the int64 tier keeps
its checked clamp (`DECIMAL(18,2) * DECIMAL(18,2)` is still
`DECIMAL(18,4)`), so TPC-H is unaffected (SF1 `sum(l_extendedprice *
l_discount)` is within noise of main). The most visible consequence:
`sum()` over a narrow decimal returns `DECIMAL(38,s)`, so arithmetic on
a sum is now wide, e.g. `sum(l_extendedprice) * 2` is `DECIMAL(48,2)`;
such results are computed on aggregated rows, but clients see a wide
decimal where they used to see a 128-bit one (the C API `duckdb_decimal`
cannot hold it, Arrow needs `decimal256`, i.e. `arrow_output_version`
1.1 or later). A `HUGEINT` is treated as 39 decimal digits by the
safe-cast pushdown, since `DECIMAL(39,0)` holds every value.
* **Wide `SUM`.** The sum of a wide `DECIMAL(w, s)` is `DECIMAL(w + 20,
s)`: 20 digits hold the sum of any number of rows (below 2^64), so it
never overflows and needs no check.
* **Division.** `/` keeps returning `DOUBLE`, as for every other
decimal. `//` keeps skipping decimals.

### What works

* Type binding of any width up to `max_decimal_width`
(`DECIMAL(300,100)`, `DECIMAL(1000,0)`, and `DECIMAL(4294967295,0)` once
the setting is raised), literals (an unquoted literal of any length is
an exact decimal: `typeof(12345678901234567890123456789012345678.5)` is
`DECIMAL(39,1)` instead of `DOUBLE`, a 1000-digit literal is
`DECIMAL(1001,1)`; literals with an exponent stay `DOUBLE`), `CREATE
TABLE`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, primary keys and indexes,
checkpoint and reload, CSV import/export (including `decimal_separator`
and `thousands`), JSON transform (numbers and strings).
* Casts: VARCHAR (with exponent notation, rounding half away from zero,
whitespace, underscores), all integer types, HUGEINT/UHUGEINT,
FLOAT/DOUBLE (a double is converted exactly; a wide value beyond the
range of the target is an out-of-range error, like `BIGNUM -> DOUBLE`,
and `NULL` for `TRY_CAST`), BOOLEAN, BIGNUM (both directions, both
tiers), fixed-size <-> wide decimals with rescaling and range checks,
`TRY_CAST`.
* Arithmetic and functions: `+`, `-`, unary `-`, `*`, `%`, `abs`,
comparisons, `BETWEEN`, `IN`, `greatest`/`least`, `CASE`,
`round`/`round_even`/`ceil`/`floor`/`trunc` (returning `DECIMAL` under
the same rules as the narrow tiers; a negative precision always has room
to carry).
* Aggregates: `SUM` (`DECIMAL(w + 20, s)`), `AVG` (exact BIGNUM sum, one
final division, so `DECIMAL(39,10)` and `DECIMAL(38,10)` of the same
values average identically; beyond the range of a `long double` the
exact sum is divided by the count before it becomes a `DOUBLE`, so the
average of values near `1e308` stays finite, and the optimizer keeps a
wide `avg` native instead of rewriting it to `sum / count`), `MIN`,
`MAX`, `COUNT`, `FIRST`/`LAST`/`ANY_VALUE`, `ARG_MIN`/`ARG_MAX`, `LIST`,
`quantile_disc` (exact), window functions including `FILL` (the exact
delta scaled by the slope like the hugeint tier, exactly beyond the
`DOUBLE` range with the power of two of that scaling as a BIGNUM, so a
slope down to the smallest denormal keeps every mantissa bit; an
extrapolation truncates the filled value like the hugeint tier and only
the result is checked against the width). The sum and avg states export
and import (`verify_aggregate_state_export`). `median`/`quantile_cont`,
`approx_quantile` and `reservoir_quantile` interpolate through `DOUBLE`,
as they do for the narrow tiers.
* **VARIANT.** Wide decimals are held by the existing `DECIMAL` variant
kind; above 38 digits the payload is a length-prefixed BIGNUM blob
instead of a fixed-size integer, width and scale are varints. Casts in
both directions, `variant_typeof`/`variant_extract`, JSON, comparison
and shredding (typed wide columns only at storage version 2.1.0 or
later) work. The Parquet VARIANT specification stops at 38 digits, so
the Parquet writer does not shred wide decimals and raises a clear error
for them.
* **Parquet.** Wide decimals are written as `FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY` two's
complement with min/max statistics, and read back; `DECIMAL` columns
with any precision above 38 (e.g. BigQuery `BIGDECIMAL`) are now read as
wide decimals instead of `DOUBLE`, with exact zonemap statistics.
Parquet's precision is an `int32`, which the writer reports as the one
bound of that format.
* **Arrow.** Wide decimals up to 76 digits are exported as `decimal256`
(requires `arrow_output_version` 1.1 or later; the default 1.0 gives a
clear error) and `decimal256` arrays are imported as wide decimals, or
as fixed-size decimals when their precision is at most 38.
* **C API (v1 and v2) and Appender.** The `uint8_t` fields and
parameters of `duckdb_decimal`, `duckdb_create_decimal_type`,
`duckdb_create_decimal`, `duckdb_bind_decimal`,
`duckdb_double_to_decimal`, `duckdb_get_decimal` and the deprecated
`duckdb_value_*` fetches reach widths up to 255, the bound that belongs
to that format; `duckdb_decimal_width`/`duckdb_decimal_scale` report 0
for a wider type and the fetches return their usual "cannot be
converted" zero value, with the exact value available through the
VARCHAR fetches. `duckdb_decimal_internal_type` reports
`DUCKDB_TYPE_BIGNUM` for wide decimals, which is what their vectors
hold. A `duckdb_decimal` carries a `duckdb_hugeint`, so a wide value is
reported through it only when its unscaled value fits in 128 bits. In
the v2 API `value_create_decimal` takes its `uint8_t` widths up to 255,
`value_get_decimal` reports the backing integer when it fits and fails
with an error otherwise (also for a width beyond 255), `value_get_blob`
hands out the exact BIGNUM storage of a wide decimal for
`bignum_decode`, and the type parameters of a DECIMAL are `UINTEGER`
values. The Appender's typed appends reach wide columns. The C++
extension wrapper (`tools/cpp/duckdb_cpp.hpp`) reports a DECIMAL's width
and scale as `uint32_t` (`GetDecimalWidth`/`GetDecimalScale`) and
`BIGNUM` as the internal type of a wide decimal
(`GetDecimalInternalTypeId`). `Decimal::MAX_WIDTH_DECIMAL` stays defined
as 38, the widest fixed-size tier, because out-of-tree extensions
(ducklake, glue, legacy_parser, postgres, sqlite) use it; it is no
longer a bound inside the engine.

### API change

New session setting `max_decimal_width` (UBIGINT, default 1000000).
`DecimalType::MaxWidth()` returns the `uint32_t` maximum,
`Decimal::MaxWidth(context)` the bound of the session, and
`Decimal::CheckedWidth` takes the context. The DECIMAL type
constructor's `width` and `scale` parameters are `UINTEGER` (they were
`UTINYINT`), which `duckdb_types()` reports, and the v2 C API's DECIMAL
type parameters are `UINTEGER` values.

### Not supported yet (clear `NotImplementedException` instead of a
silent wrong result)

`decimal_division`, Arrow export above 76 digits, wide decimals inside
Parquet VARIANT (a specification limit), Parquet precisions beyond
`int32`.

### Tests

`test/sql/types/decimal/wide_decimal_{casts,arithmetic,storage,statistics,literals,aggregates,rounding,review,index_storage_version,catalog_storage_version,stored_expressions,aggregate_state_storage_version,unbounded_width,unbounded_statistics}.test`
cover type binding, every cast direction with rounding and range errors,
the promotion rules, persistence across a restart, exact statistics and
row-group pruning per operator, joins, grouping, aggregates (including
the avg equality between tiers), rounding against the `DECIMAL(38)`
results, windows, primary keys, the storage-version gates (columns,
types, macros, views, defaults, aggregate states, looping over storage
versions 1.4.0 and 2.0.0) and the legacy index keys and macro defaults,
CSV, Parquet round trip and statistics, and widths well beyond 255
(`DECIMAL(300,100)`, `DECIMAL(1000,500)`, `DECIMAL(4294967295,0)`, a
1000-digit literal, 600-digit products, the `uint32_t` ceiling).
`test/sql/types/decimal/wide_decimal_long_arithmetic.test` covers
products of 1500- to 4000-digit factors against the exact values,
20,000-digit round trips through VARCHAR and BIGNUM, rescaling by powers
of ten of thousands of digits and a conversion interrupted by
`max_execution_time`; `test/sql/settings/max_decimal_width.test` covers
the setting (type binding, casts, literals, arithmetic, `sum`, `round`
and common-type bounds, the 38-digit legacy behaviour, columns written
under a larger bound).
`test/sql/types/variant/variant_wide_decimal.test` covers VARIANT (round
trip, typeof, extract, JSON, ordering, shredded storage with restart,
the Parquet boundary). `bigdecimal.test` asserts the exact values,
`csv_wide_decimal_separator.test` the CSV separators, and
`pushdown_safe_decimal_cast.test` the HUGEINT cases. A wide-decimal
query was added to the existing Arrow round-trip test, wide cases to the
existing C API value, type and appender tests, and the existing tests
that asserted "width must be between 1 and 38", "DECIMAL cannot be cast
to BIGNUM" or an overflow / scale truncation at the 38-digit boundary
were updated to the exact results.

### Indexes stored before wide decimals

The engines of the storage versions before wide decimals bind every
decimal index key within 38 digits (`(a + b)` over `DECIMAL(38,2)`
columns is a `DECIMAL(38,2)` key), and the keys they store have those
types; here the same key binds to the wide `DECIMAL(39,2)`, whose keys
would not match the stored ones, so a `UNIQUE` index would silently
accept duplicates. An index records the storage version it was created
under (the ART has saved it since v1.5.0, an index without it predates
that), and binding a stored index whose recorded version predates wide
decimals refuses a key that binds to a wide decimal with a `Binder
Error` that names the index, the key and both types and says to `DROP
INDEX` and `CREATE` it again (with the key cast to at most 38 digits, or
after upgrading the database to storage version 2.1.0); indexes whose
key types do not change, such as an index on a plain column, bind as
before, and nothing is rebuilt silently. Conversely `CREATE INDEX`
refuses a wide decimal key in a database of an older storage version,
like a wide column ("DECIMAL index keys wider than 38 digits are not
supported in storage versions prior to v2.1.0"), so the engines of that
version read every index with the key types they bind.
`test/sql/storage/bc/test_decimal_expression_index_v2_0.test` opens
`data/storage/decimal_expression_index_{v1_4_0,v2_0_0}.db.gz`, written
by a DuckDB before wide decimals with a `UNIQUE` index on `(a + b)` and
one on `a`, and asserts the error, the working column index, the
re-creation with a cast key and the upgrade path. Binding expressions as
an older engine did in general is cross-version compatibility beyond
wide decimals and left for a separate change.

Note: this PR was generated by an AI coding agent and reviewed by the
author.
subject: Support DECIMAL widths beyond 38 digits, stored as BIGNUM blobs (#26955)

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
## Problem

Several catalog commands reject nested schema paths or use only the last
schema name. This can list tables from the wrong schema, bind a foreign
key to the wrong table, or produce misleading errors. Data generators
can also load or replace tables in the wrong schema. `USE`, `schema` and
`search_path` also reject nested schemas.

The SQL below sets up `lake` with a nested
`s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail` schema and a top-level `retail`
schema. We use this setup in the examples for each issue and its fix.
Each fix has its own commit.

```sql
ATTACH ':memory:' AS lake;
USE lake;
CREATE SCHEMA lake.s3tablescatalog;
CREATE SCHEMA lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo;
CREATE SCHEMA lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail;
CREATE SCHEMA lake.retail;
CREATE TABLE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.widget_sales AS SELECT 42 AS id;
CREATE TABLE lake.retail.other AS SELECT 7 AS id;
```

## SHOW TABLES

The first two commands previously failed in the parser. The third
included `widget_sales` from the nested schema. They now resolve the
full path and filter by schema identity.

```sql
SHOW TABLES FROM lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail; -- widget_sales
SHOW TABLES FROM s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail;      -- widget_sales
SHOW TABLES FROM lake.retail;                          -- only other
```

Prepared `SHOW TABLES` statements also follow later `USE` changes.
`PRAGMA show_tables` now goes through the same binder, including when
prepared through the C++ API.

```sql
PREPARE list_tables AS SHOW TABLES;
USE lake.retail;
EXECUTE list_tables; -- only other
USE lake;
```

The same behavior applies to an API-prepared pragma:

```cpp
con.Query("USE lake");
auto tables = con.Prepare("PRAGMA show_tables");
con.Query("USE lake.retail");
auto result = tables->Execute(); // only other
con.Query("USE lake");
```

Schema IDs are resolved again when a prepared statement runs. Dropping
and recreating the schema no longer leaves `SHOW TABLES FROM` with a
stale ID.

```sql
CREATE SCHEMA lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.recreated;
PREPARE list_recreated AS SHOW TABLES FROM lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.recreated;
DROP SCHEMA lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.recreated;
CREATE SCHEMA lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.recreated;
CREATE TABLE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.recreated.t(i INTEGER);
EXECUTE list_recreated; -- t
DROP SCHEMA lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.recreated CASCADE;
```

`SHOW ALL TABLES` also merged same-named objects from schemas with the
same leaf name. It now groups tables and views by their object IDs.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lake.retail.widget_sales(id INTEGER, v VARCHAR);
SHOW ALL TABLES;
-- Two widget_sales rows, with [id] and [id, v] as their column lists.
```

## DROP SEQUENCE and DROP INDEX

Creation already worked, but the corresponding `DROP` commands rejected
the longer names. Both pairs now succeed. The parser generator renumbers
its shared tables when the index rule changes, which accounts for most
of the generated diff.

```sql
CREATE SEQUENCE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.seq;
DROP SEQUENCE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.seq;

CREATE INDEX idx ON lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.widget_sales(id);
DROP INDEX lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.idx;
```

## USE, schema and search_path

These commands previously rejected nested schemas. They now retain the
full path, so unqualified reads and creates use the selected schema.
`SHOW SCHEMAS` marks that schema as current, including in prepared
statements. The change reuses the existing search-path representation.

```sql
USE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail;
SELECT * FROM widget_sales; -- 42
SHOW TABLES; -- only widget_sales
SELECT database_name, schema_name FROM (SHOW SCHEMAS) WHERE current;
-- lake, retail: exactly one current row, for the selected nested schema.

USE s3tablescatalog.salesdemo;
SELECT current_schema(); -- s3tablescatalog.salesdemo

SET schema = 'lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail';
SELECT * FROM widget_sales; -- 42
CREATE TABLE created_here AS SELECT 99 AS id;
SELECT * FROM lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.created_here; -- 99

SET search_path = 'lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail';
SELECT * FROM widget_sales; -- 42

USE lake; -- Reset the default for the following examples.
```

A schema found through another catalog's search-path entry now retains
that catalog. Previously, `USE` could succeed but store the schema under
the default catalog, where it did not exist.

```sql
ATTACH ':memory:' AS other;
SET search_path = 'other.main,lake.s3tablescatalog';
USE s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail;
CREATE TABLE resolved_here AS SELECT 123 AS id;
SELECT * FROM lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.resolved_here; -- 123
USE lake;
DETACH other;
```

Remote pushdown checks now use the full local schema path too. With a
remote catalog also in the search path, the local lookup for
`widget_sales` checks `lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail`. The
previous check used `lake.retail`.

## dbgen and dsdgen

After `USE` selected a nested schema, `dbgen` and `dsdgen` still
targeted the top-level schema with the same last name.
`dsdgen(overwrite=true)` could replace an existing table there. Both
generators now carry the full schema path through binding, table
creation, and data loading.

```sql
LOAD tpch;
LOAD tpcds;
CREATE TABLE lake.retail.customer_address AS SELECT 42 AS sentinel;
USE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail;
CALL dbgen(sf=0.01, suffix='_tpch');
CALL dsdgen(sf=0, overwrite=true);
SELECT sentinel FROM lake.retail.customer_address; -- still 42
SELECT count(*) FROM lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.nation_tpch; -- 25
SELECT count(*) FROM lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.customer_address; -- 0
USE lake;
```

`schema=` follows core's string-schema rules. It prefers an existing
nested path and falls back to a literal name. Explicit double quotes
select the literal name. Resolution uses the final `catalog=` value,
regardless of parameter order.

```sql
CREATE SCHEMA lake.retail.reporting;
CREATE SCHEMA lake."retail.reporting";
CALL dbgen(sf=0, schema='retail.reporting');   -- lake.retail.reporting
CALL dbgen(sf=0, schema='"retail.reporting"'); -- lake."retail.reporting"
```

## Foreign keys

A reference could silently bind to a different table when both schemas
ended in `retail`. These commands now report the existing cross-schema
error in both directions.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lake.retail.pk(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.pk(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);

CREATE TABLE lake.retail.fk(
    id INTEGER REFERENCES lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.pk(id)
);
CREATE TABLE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.fk(
    id INTEGER REFERENCES lake.retail.pk(id)
);
```

Valid references within the same schema retain their full path in the
saved constraint SQL, including after reopening the database.

```sql
CREATE TABLE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.fk(
    id INTEGER REFERENCES s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.pk(id)
);
-- Saved constraint: REFERENCES s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.pk(id)
```

## Schemas under main

The lookup for `main.sub.t` previously selected `temp.main` and failed.
It now resolves against the default database.

```sql
CREATE SCHEMA lake.main.sub;
CREATE TABLE lake.main.sub.t AS SELECT 7 AS i;
SELECT * FROM main.sub.t; -- 7, as with lake.main.sub.t
```

## Missing-entry errors and suggestions

A missing nested function previously reported that the first schema
component was a missing catalog. The error now identifies the missing
function. Suggestions also include the full nested path.

```sql
SELECT s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.nope(1);
-- Scalar Function with name nope does not exist.

CREATE TABLE lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.example_table(id INTEGER);
SELECT * FROM example_tabl;
-- Did you mean "lake.s3tablescatalog.salesdemo.retail.example_table"?
```

## Catalogs without nested-schema support

An extension that discards parent schema names can read or modify the
wrong object. Core now rejects nested paths when the catalog reports
`SupportsNestedSchemas() == false`. The check covers entry lookup,
schema-path lookup, schema creation and dropping, and remote pushdown
before it bypasses normal binding.

For an attached catalog `ext` without nested-schema support, these
statements fail with a clear unsupported-schema error:

```sql
SELECT * FROM ext.a.b.t;
CREATE TABLE ext.a.b.t3(i INTEGER);
USE ext.a.b;
CREATE SCHEMA ext.a.b;
DROP SCHEMA ext.a.b CASCADE;
```

The error includes the rejected schema path. If `ext` is the default
catalog, a misspelled catalog name such as `lakee` is interpreted as a
parent schema. The message now shows that interpretation:

```sql
USE ext;
SELECT * FROM lakee.sales.t;
-- Catalog "ext" does not support nested schemas: lakee.sales
```

`ext."a.b".t` still names one literal schema, so the guard does not
reject it. Quack now declares the nested-schema support it already
implements. DuckLake already declares support for 1.1 metadata; its 1.0
test accepts the earlier core error.

## Validation

Built with `FORCE_DEBUG=1 FORCE_ASSERT=1` after merging `main`. The
focused run passed 42 test cases with 1,890 assertions. One parser test
was skipped because autocomplete is unavailable. Coverage includes
nested catalog commands, search paths, prepared SHOW statements,
unsupported extension catalogs, Quack nested-schema lookup and DDL/DML,
and DuckLake metadata 1.0 and 1.1 behavior.

The error-message follow-up passed the catalog capability regression and
DuckLake version gate with 185 assertions. The checks cover mistyped
catalog names, full schema paths, and identifier quoting through entry
lookup, schema lookup, CREATE/DROP SCHEMA, and remote pushdown.

Nine focused TPCH/TPCDS tests passed with 263 assertions. They cover
both generation modes, overwrite protection, named-schema resolution and
quoting, catalog-parameter order, read-only catalogs, and existing
generation behavior. The new regressions reproduced the failures before
the fixes. Clang-tidy passed on the changed binding lines.

The parser trampoline was regenerated from the merged grammar.
Formatting and extension patch checks passed. Full-suite validation is
left to CI.
subject: Fix nested schema resolution in catalog commands and search paths (#28771)

author: Mark <mark@ducklabs.com>
message:
A plain CREATE of a repository that exists used to fail whatever it
asked for, so a script could not state "this repository, with this
definition" without IF NOT EXISTS (which keeps any definition) or OR
REPLACE (which overwrites). Now it returns the stored repository when
the request describes it, and names the difference otherwise:
- without a prefix the request only names a host, so it matches a
repository that was resolved from that host;
- with a prefix, the prefix must match (a trailing slash aside) and so
must the keys when the request gives any; keys that are not given were
fetched from the prefix and are not fetched again. Nothing here reaches
the network: what the host or the prefix serve today is checked only by
OR REPLACE. The strict "fail if anything is there" is still DROP without
IF EXISTS followed by CREATE.

The conflict is now decided before the opt-in
(allow_extension_repositories): returning what is stored adds no trust,
and a request for something else is reported as the difference it is,
whatever the access level. Only a statement that would add or overwrite
a repository is subject to the opt-in; a locked configuration still
refuses everything.

This makes that repeated:
```sql
CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY carlopi.github.io;
```
(same session or different sessions) succeed, and that allows script or
documentation pages to restate the `CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY` that
will double as assertion that stuff is (after a successfull statement)
properly set-up.
subject: CREATE EXTENSION REPOSITORY passes when it asks for the repository that is already stored (#28862)

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
hunk_contexts: void Node7Leaf::InsertByte(ART &art, NodePtr &node_ptr, const uint8_t byte) {
void Node4::InsertChild(ART &art, NodePtr &node_ptr, const uint8_t byte, const N
void NodePtr::InsertChild(ART &art, NodePtr &node_ptr, const uint8_t byte, const
void PrefixHandle::Append(ART &art, PrefixHandle prefix, NodePtr other_ptr) {
message:
https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/11022

Final step for porting ART deletion. Ports the traversal in
ARTOperator::Delete to pinned handles. The legacy version kept unpinned
references to the NodePtrs of the current node and its three ancestors
across the whole descent, and read nodes through the raw accessors.

Unlike Insert, Delete passes NodePtrs to callees that may free the node
storing them:
1. Node7Leaf::DeleteByte frees the gate prefix storing the Node7Leaf's
NodePtr.
2. Concat can free the prefix chain storing the Node4's NodePtr.

So Insert's approach, a NodeHandle in the caller's scope plus a NodePtr
reference into it, doesn't work here, since the caller would still hold
the pin while the callee frees the node. Passing the pin and the
reference separately would work, but every callee and every step down
the tree then has to keep the two in sync by hand, and nothing catches a
reference that outlives its pin.

This reintroduces NodePtrHandle, which pairs a NodePtr reference with
the pin on the node storing it (NodeHandle pins the node a NodePtr
points to, NodePtrHandle pins the node that contains the NodePtr). The
reference can only be created from the pin, and releasing the handle
drops both. In #25487 we removed the earlier version in favor of plain
RAII and agreed to only bring it back where it's actually needed, so
it's limited to Delete and its callees (NodePtr::DeleteChild,
Node4::DeleteChild, Node7Leaf::DeleteByte and PrefixHandle::Concat),
which take it by value and either write through it, release it before
the free, or take over its pin. Only ARTOperator can create an unpinned
handle, for the root NodePtr, which isn't stored in buffer memory.

Delete keeps a fixed window of four handles that moves down one level
per prefix chain or inner node, so the number of pins doesn't grow with
the key length. Concat now gets the handle to the NodePtr that pointed
to the freed Node4, which already pins the tail of the parent's prefix
chain, so this also removes PrefixHandle::GetTail.
subject: Buffer managed indexes 5d delete traversal (#28867)

author: Laurens Kuiper <laurens@ducklabs.com>
message:
Closes https://github.com/duckdblabs/duckdb-internal/issues/11281

PR from https://github.com/duckdb-bot/duckdb/pull/107

Updating a `VARIANT` column with a nested JSON constant took time
quadratic in the nesting depth, and deeper values failed with `VARIANT
exceeds maximum recursion depth of 128`. Inserting the same value was
not affected.

The optimizer folds the cast into a `VARIANT` constant.
`RelationStatisticsHelper` then named each projection, group and
aggregate column with `GetName()`, and for an unaliased constant that
renders the value through `Value::ToSQLString`. Nothing reads these
names except `RelationManager::PrintRelationStats`, and nothing calls
that. This PR passes an empty `Identifier()` at the three call sites
instead.

At 64 levels, the `UPDATE` drops from ~11 s to 0.03 s on a release
build. The segfault in the JSON → VARIANT cast reported in the issue
does not reproduce on `main` anymore.

Tests:
- `test/optimizer/relation_statistics.cpp`: calls the projection and
aggregate statistics helpers directly with a 1,000-level constant, and
runs `UPDATE`, `first()`, `GROUP BY` and `INSERT ... SELECT` with it.
The SQL test is skipped in debug builds, because
`LogicalOperator::Verify` renders every plan expression there and fails
at this depth.
- `test/issues/general/test_25967.test`: the `UPDATE` from the issue,
kept shallow enough for debug builds.

Not in this PR: `EXPLAIN` and profiling still render the constant, so
they are still slow on these values and fail on very deep ones.
subject: Stop rendering expressions as SQL to name relation statistics columns (#28803)
